title: Syllabus
text:
Course Objectives
This course introduces the mathematical principles underlying diffusion-based generative models used in modern AI. Students will learn how noise is progressively added to data and how neural networks are trained to reverse this process to generate realistic samples. The course builds on probability, Gaussian distributions, and optimization to explain diffusion processes, denoising objectives, and sampling algorithms. Emphasis is placed on intuitive derivations, geometric interpretation of probability distributions, and connections to familiar machine learning concepts such as maximum likelihood and variational inference. By the end of the course, students will understand diffusion models both conceptually and mathematically.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course Outcomes
At the end of this course, students will be able to:

Explain the forward and reverse diffusion processes.
Derive the Gaussian noise perturbation model used in diffusion models.
Understand and interpret the denoising training objective.
Connect diffusion models with likelihood-based learning.
Implement and analyze simplified diffusion sampling algorithms.
Compare diffusion models with GANs and VAEs.
Read and interpret recent diffusion model research papers.

title: Probability 101 — A Refresher
text:
The sample space, events, and the probability measure
A random experiment is modeled by three objects.
All further rules are consequences of the axioms; two used constantly are \(P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)\) and \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\).
A remark on the continuous case. For \(\Omega = [0,1]\) with the uniform measure, every singleton event \(\{\omega\}\) has probability zero, although some outcome certainly occurs. Probability zero therefore does not mean impossibility; it means a vanishing fraction of the possibilities. This is also the reason \(P\) is defined on events rather than on individual outcomes: in the continuous case, individual outcomes are too small to carry probability.

title: Probability 101 — A Refresher
text:
The sample space \(\Omega\) is the set of all possible outcomes of the experiment, with one element \(\omega \in \Omega\) per complete outcome. For a single die, \(\Omega = \{1, \dots, 6\}\). For two coin tosses, \(\Omega = \{HH, HT, TH, TT\}\); note that an outcome specifies the result of the entire experiment, i.e. both tosses. For a point drawn from the interval \([0,1]\), \(\Omega = [0,1]\), an uncountable set.
An event is a subset \(A \subseteq \Omega\); events are the objects to which probabilities are assigned. “The die shows an even number” is the event \(\{2, 4, 6\}\); “at least one head” is the event \(\{HH, HT, TH\}\). An event is a collection of outcomes, not an outcome.
The probability measure is the first of the two maps:
\[
P : \text{events} \longrightarrow [0, 1],
\]
required to satisfy Kolmogorov’s axioms: (i) \(P(A) \ge 0\) for every event \(A\);

\(P(\Omega) = 1\); (iii) for mutually exclusive events \(A_1, A_2, \dots\), \(P\big(\bigcup_i A_i\big) = \sum_i P(A_i)\) (countable additivity).

title: Probability 101 — A Refresher
text:
Random variables
The second map is the random variable. A random variable is a function
\[
X : \Omega \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}
\]
that assigns a numerical value to each outcome. For the two-coin experiment with \(X\) the number of heads: \(X(HH) = 2\), \(X(HT) = X(TH) = 1\), \(X(TT) = 0\). Despite the name, \(X\) is a fixed, deterministic function; the randomness resides entirely in which outcome \(\omega\) the experiment produces.
The two maps combine as follows. A statement such as \(\mathbb{P}(X = 1)\) is evaluated by first identifying the event determined by the condition and then applying \(P\) to it:
\[
\mathbb{P}(X = 1)
\;=\; P\big(\{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) = 1\}\big)
\;=\; P(\{HT, TH\}) = \tfrac{2}{4}.
\]
Carrying this out for every value (or set of values) of \(X\) yields the distribution of \(X\), a probability assignment on the real line. Once the distribution is available, the underlying sample space is usually suppressed and one works with the distribution directly; this is standard practice, and the remainder of the course follows it. The present section records what that convention leaves implicit.
A discrete random variable is described by its probability mass function (pmf) \(p(x) = \mathbb{P}(X = x)\), with \(\sum_x p(x) = 1\). A continuous random variable is described by its probability density function (pdf) \(f(x) \ge 0\), with \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\, dx = 1\); probabilities are obtained as areas under the density,
\[
\mathbb{P}(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\, dx .
\]
Three properties of densities deserve emphasis.

A density value is not a probability and may exceed 1; the Uniform distribution on \([0, \tfrac12]\) has \(f \equiv 2\). Only areas under the density are probabilities.
\(\mathbb{P}(X = x) = 0\) for every individual \(x\), by the singleton remark above. The informal reading of a density is \(f(x)\,dx \approx\) the probability of an outcome within \(dx\) of \(x\); densities compare the relative plausibility of neighborhoods.
The cumulative distribution function (CDF) \(F(x) = \mathbb{P}(X \le x)\) applies to discrete and continuous variables alike, and its derivative, where it exists, is the pdf. The CDF appears in Generative AI, in Its Simplest Form as the sampling map \(F^{-1}\).

Joint distributions
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be two random variables defined on the same sample space — two numerical features of the same outcome. Their joint distribution specifies \(p(x, y) = \mathbb{P}(X = x \text{ and } Y = y)\) in the discrete case, or a joint density \(f(x, y)\) whose volumes are probabilities in the continuous case. The joint distribution is a complete description of the pair: every probabilistic statement about \((X, Y)\) can be computed from it.

title: Probability 101 — A Refresher
text:
Marginal distributions
The marginal distribution of \(X\) describes \(X\) alone, with \(Y\) disregarded. It is obtained by summing (or, for densities, integrating) the joint distribution over the other variable:
\[
p(x) = \sum_y p(x, y),
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
f(x) = \int f(x, y)\, dy .
\]
In the table these are the row and column sums — the margins of the table, which is the origin of the term: \(\mathbb{P}(\text{cloudy}) = 0.45\) and \(\mathbb{P}(\text{rain}) = 0.25\). The operation is justified directly by the additivity axiom: the event “cloudy” is the disjoint union of “cloudy and rain” and “cloudy and no rain”. Marginalization recurs throughout the course; in the mixture model of Generative AI, in Its Simplest Form, the observed density \(p(x) = \sum_z p(z)\, p(x \mid z)\) is precisely the joint distribution of \((x, z)\) with the latent variable summed out.

title: Probability 101 — A Refresher
text:
Conditional distributions and Bayes’ rule
The conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X = x\) is defined, whenever \(p(x) > 0\), by
\[
p(y \mid x) = \frac{p(x, y)}{p(x)} .
\]
The definition restricts attention to the outcomes consistent with \(X = x\) and renormalizes their probabilities to total 1. In the running example, \(\mathbb{P}(\text{rain} \mid \text{cloudy}) = 0.20 / 0.45 \approx 0.44\), compared with the unconditional \(\mathbb{P}(\text{rain}) = 0.25\).
Applying the definition in both directions and eliminating the joint yields Bayes’ rule,
\[
\boxed{\;p(x \mid y) = \frac{p(y \mid x)\, p(x)}{p(y)}\;}
\]
which converts a conditional in one direction into the conditional in the other. The tanh denoiser of W01 is an application of this identity, with \(x\) the clean data point and \(y\) the noisy observation.
\(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if \(p(x, y) = p(x)\, p(y)\) for all \(x, y\) — equivalently, if \(p(y \mid x) = p(y)\), so that conditioning on \(X\) conveys no information about \(Y\). In the table, \(0.20 \ne 0.45 \times 0.25\), so the two variables are dependent. The i.i.d. assumption underlying the likelihoods of Distributions and Maximum Likelihood are an independence statement applied to repeated observations.

title: Probability 101 — A Refresher
text:
Expectation
The expectation of a random variable is the probability-weighted average of its values,
\[
\mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_x x\, p(x)
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\mathbb{E}[X] = \int x\, f(x)\, dx ,
\]
the center of mass of the distribution. The expectation need not be an attainable value; a fair die has \(\mathbb{E}[X] = 3.5\). More generally, for a function \(g\),
\[
\mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \sum_x g(x)\, p(x)
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\int g(x)\, f(x)\, dx ,
\]
so that the distribution of \(g(X)\) itself need never be computed (a fact sometimes called the law of the unconscious statistician).
Two properties carry most of the weight in this course.

Linearity. \(\mathbb{E}[aX + bY] = a\,\mathbb{E}[X] + b\,\mathbb{E}[Y]\) holds for all random variables on a common sample space, with no independence assumption. (Independence is required for the separate statement \(\mathbb{E}[XY] = \mathbb{E}[X]\,\mathbb{E}[Y]\).)
Variance. \(\operatorname{Var}(X) =
\mathbb{E}\big[(X - \mathbb{E}X)^2\big] =
\mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}X)^2\) measures spread about the mean, and for independent random variables variances add. The identity \(\operatorname{Var}(x_0 + \sigma z) = 1 + \sigma^2\) of W01 is an instance.

Finally, the conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = y]\) is the mean of the conditional distribution of \(X\) given \(Y = y\), regarded as a function of \(y\). It is the minimum-mean-squared-error prediction of \(X\) from the observation \(Y = y\) (proved in Distributions and Maximum Likelihood), and the denoiser \(\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_\sigma]\) of W01 is precisely a conditional expectation.

Exhibit (a) a pdf exceeding 3 at some point; (b) a random variable whose expectation is not an attainable value; (c) two dependent random variables for which \(\mathbb{E}[X + Y] = \mathbb{E}[X] + \mathbb{E}[Y]\) nevertheless holds, illustrating that linearity requires no independence.

In the mixture model \(z \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi)\), \(x \mid z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_z, \sigma^2)\): identify the joint \(p(x, z)\), both marginals, and both conditionals. title: Distributions and Maximum Likelihood
text:
How sampling actually works
Every sampler in the playground reduces to uniform random numbers:

Inverse CDF. If \(F\) is a CDF and \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\), then \(X = F^{-1}(U)\) has CDF \(F\) (proved in the companion note Generative AI, in Its Simplest Form). This handles Uniform (\(x = a + (b-a)u\)) and anything with a computable \(F^{-1}\).
Box–Muller for the Normal: with \(U_1, U_2\) independent uniforms, \(\sqrt{-2\log U_1}\,\cos(2\pi U_2)\) is exactly \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\). This is the sampler inside every demo of this course.
Pick-then-sample for mixtures: draw the component index with probabilities \(\pi_i\), then sample that component — ancestral sampling, the subject of the companion note.
Gamma and Beta use clever rejection samplers (the playground uses Marsaglia–Tsang); we treat them as black boxes.

title: Distributions and Maximum Likelihood
text:
Likelihood
Fix a family \(f(x;\theta)\) and observe an i.i.d. dataset \(x_1, \dots, x_n\). The likelihood and log-likelihood are
\[
L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i; \theta),
\qquad
\ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log f(x_i; \theta),
\]
and the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) is \(\hat\theta = \arg\max_\theta \ell(\theta)\). The log changes nothing about the argmax (monotonicity) and everything about the algebra and the numerics: a product of 3000 numbers of size \(10^{-2}\) underflows; a sum of their logs is a perfectly pleasant \(\approx -13{,}800\).

The Likelihood Lens shows both as slices of the same surface \(f(x;\mu) = \mathcal{N}(x; \mu, \sigma^2)\): the horizontal slice (fix \(\mu\)) is a density in \(x\); the vertical slice (fix \(x\)) is a likelihood in \(\mu\). For the Gaussian the two slices happen to have the same bell shape, because \(f(x;\mu) = f(\mu;x)\) — a symmetry of this family, not a general fact (repeat the exercise mentally with a Gamma in \(\theta\)). What is general: the likelihood is not a probability distribution over \(\theta\) — it need not integrate to 1, and only its argmax and local shape carry meaning.

title: Distributions and Maximum Likelihood
text:
The Gaussian MLE, in full
\[
\ell(\mu, \sigma^2)
= -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)^2 .
\]
Maximize over \(\mu\). Only the second term involves \(\mu\):
\[
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \mu}
= \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)
= \frac{n}{\sigma^2}(\bar{x} - \mu)
\;\stackrel{!}{=}\; 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{\ \hat\mu = \bar{x}\ }
\]
for every \(\sigma\) — which is why, in the Lens, changing \(\sigma\) sharpens the log-likelihood parabola but never moves its peak.
Maximize over \(\sigma^2\) (treat \(v = \sigma^2\) as the variable):
\[
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial v}
= -\frac{n}{2v} + \frac{1}{2v^2}\sum_i (x_i - \hat\mu)^2
\;\stackrel{!}{=}\; 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{\ \hat\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2\ }
\]
(One should check this is a maximum, not merely critical: \(\ell \to -\infty\) as \(v \to 0^+\) and as \(v \to \infty\), and this is the only critical point.) Note the divisor \(n\): the MLE of the variance is biased — \(\mathbb{E}[\hat\sigma^2] =
\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2\) — which is where the familiar \(n-1\) estimator comes from. For this course the distinction is a footnote; the MLE is what the theory produces.

title: Distributions and Maximum Likelihood
section: Aside: binary cross-entropy is a likelihood
text:
Aside: binary cross-entropy is a likelihood
The most familiar loss in machine learning is a maximum-likelihood problem in disguise, and the disguise falls away the moment classification is read as a (conditional) generative model.
The model. For the \(i\)-th sample with features \(x_i\), model the binary label as a Bernoulli trial,
\[
y_i \mid x_i \;\sim\; \text{Bernoulli}(\pi_i), \qquad y_i \in \{0, 1\},
\]
and let a neural network supply the logit — the log-odds, not the log-probability:
\[
s_i = f_\theta(x_i) = \log \frac{\pi_i}{1 - \pi_i}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\pi_i = \operatorname{sigmoid}(s_i).
\]
The likelihood. The Bernoulli pmf can be written in one line as \(p(y \mid \pi) = \pi^{y} (1-\pi)^{1-y}\), so for independent samples
\[
L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n \pi_i^{\,y_i} (1 - \pi_i)^{1 - y_i},
\qquad
-\ell(\theta) = -\sum_{i=1}^n \Big[ y_i \log \pi_i + (1 - y_i)\log(1 - \pi_i) \Big].
\]
The right-hand side is exactly binary cross-entropy. Training a classifier with BCE is maximum likelihood for a conditional Bernoulli model whose log-odds are the network output — nothing more. (The name is also earned: \(-\ell/n\) is the cross-entropy between the empirical distribution of each label and the model’s Bernoulli.)
The \(\pm 1\) convention. With labels \(y_i \in \{-1, +1\}\), the identity \(\operatorname{sigmoid}(-s) = 1 - \operatorname{sigmoid}(s)\) collapses both cases into \(p(y_i \mid s_i) = \operatorname{sigmoid}(y_i s_i)\), and the negative log-likelihood becomes the logistic loss,
\[
-\ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log\!\big(1 + e^{-y_i s_i}\big)
\]
— the same objective, rewritten.
The connection to this course. W01’s latent posterior \(\mathbb{P}(z = 2 \mid x) = \operatorname{sigmoid}(2x/\sigma^2)\) is precisely this model with logit \(s(x) = 2x/\sigma^2\): the optimal classifier of the hidden component is a Bernoulli model whose log-odds are linear in the observation. Classification, denoising, and latent inference are all the same likelihood computation wearing different clothes.

title: Distributions and Maximum Likelihood
text:
Fitting the other families — honestly

Uniform. The likelihood is \((b-a)^{-n}\) if all points lie in \([a,b]\) and \(0\) otherwise: to maximize, squeeze the interval as tight as the data allows — \(\hat a = \min_i x_i\), \(\hat b = \max_i x_i\). (No calculus; the maximum is on the boundary of the constraint. That is Exercise 2.)
Gamma and Beta have no closed-form MLE. Setting the derivatives to zero produces equations involving the digamma function, solvable only numerically. The playground therefore uses the method of moments (MoM): equate the family’s mean and variance to the sample’s \(\bar x\) and \(s^2\) and solve —
\[
\text{Gamma: } \hat k = \frac{\bar{x}^2}{s^2},\ \ \hat\theta = \frac{s^2}{\bar{x}};
\qquad
\text{Beta: } c = \frac{\bar{x}(1-\bar{x})}{s^2} - 1,\ \
\hat\alpha = \bar{x}\,c,\ \ \hat\beta = (1-\bar{x})\,c .
\]
MoM is a respectable estimator in its own right (consistent, and a standard warm start for numerical MLE); the honest label matters because “just maximize the likelihood” quietly assumes machinery we haven’t built.
Mixtures. Even MoM gets awkward; the right tool is expectation–maximization (EM), which belongs to a later conversation. Today the mixture plays a different role — see below.

title: Distributions and Maximum Likelihood
section: The trap: right method, wrong family
text:
The trap: right method, wrong family
In the playground: generate 3000 samples from the two-bump mixture, then fit a single Normal by maximum likelihood. The fit is optimal within its family — and its peak sits exactly in the empty valley between the clusters, because the best single Gaussian matches the overall mean and variance, not the shape.
Two lessons. First, MLE optimizes within the family you chose; the choice of family is a modeling decision the likelihood cannot rescue. Second, we currently have no number that says how wrong this fit is. Constructing that number — the KL divergence, and its identity with maximum likelihood — is the next lecture.

title: Distributions and Maximum Likelihood
text:
Exercises

Re-derive \(\hat\sigma^2\) for the Gaussian, including the argument that the critical point is a maximum.
Show that the Uniform MLE is \((\hat a, \hat b) = (\min_i x_i, \max_i x_i)\), and explain why calculus alone would miss it.
Derive the Gamma method-of-moments estimators from \(\mathbb{E}X = k\theta\) and \(\operatorname{Var} X = k\theta^2\).
For a single observation \(x\) from \(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma\) known, sketch the likelihood in \(\mu\). Now hold \(\mu\) known and sketch the likelihood in \(\sigma\) — is it bell-shaped? Symmetric? (This kills the “likelihood looks like a pdf” illusion outside the Gaussian-mean case.)
BCE gradient. For the Bernoulli model of the aside with a linear logit \(s_i = \theta^\top x_i\), show that \(\nabla_\theta(-\ell) = \sum_i (\pi_i - y_i)\, x_i\) — prediction error times input, the cleanest gradient in machine learning. Verify that the \(\pm 1\) logistic form gives the same gradient.
For a mixture \(\sum_i \pi_i f_i\) with component means \(\mu_i\) and variances \(\sigma_i^2\), show \(\operatorname{Var}(X) = \sum_i \pi_i \sigma_i^2 + \sum_i \pi_i (\mu_i - \bar\mu)^2\) with \(\bar\mu = \sum_i \pi_i \mu_i\) — within-component plus between-component spread. Use it to predict what \(\hat\sigma\) the single-Gaussian fit in the trap will report.

title: Moving Distributions: The Transport Story
text:
The problem, without any symbols
You have a pile of examples — photographs, sentences, measurements. Behind them stands a distribution: the invisible shape that says which examples are common, which are rare, which are impossible. Generative modeling is one wish:
Here is the reframing that unlocks everything. A computer already owns one perfect source of randomness — dull, structureless randomness, like a uniform lottery number or television static. So the wish becomes a moving job:
Every generative model you have heard of — VAEs, GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion models — is a machine for doing exactly this. They differ only in how they decide which grain of sand goes where. That difference is the whole story.

title: Moving Distributions: The Transport Story
text:
Make more examples with the same shape.



Take the boring randomness we have, and transport it onto the interesting shape we want. Move the pile of sand into the sculpture.

title: Moving Distributions: The Transport Story
section: In one dimension, the problem is completely solved
text:
In one dimension, the problem is completely solved
Suppose your data is just numbers — heights, incomes, temperatures. One dimension. Then there is a classical trick, and it settles everything.
The rank trick. To transform lottery numbers into incomes:

Draw a uniform lottery number between 0 and 1 — say \(0.83\).
Read it as a rank: “the 83rd percentile.”
Output the income that sits at the 83rd percentile of the income distribution.

That’s the entire generator. Ask “what fraction of the data lies below this value?” — that question is the CDF, and it converts values into ranks. Answer it backwards — rank into value — and that is the inverse CDF. The generator is: uniform randomness in, read as a rank, matched to the value with the same rank.
Three things make this trick special, not just convenient:

It always works. Any distribution of numbers, however lumpy, has percentiles.
It is fair, and it never crosses. The 20th percentile of the lottery goes to the 20th percentile of incomes, the 90th to the 90th. Lower stays lower, higher stays higher — two grains of sand never swap places in flight.
It is the only such rule — if you insist on never crossing. Drop that insistence and even one dimension has many transports (flip every rank, \(u \leftrightarrow 1-u\), and the output distribution is identical). What is special about one dimension is not that transport is unique — it is that the line comes with a natural tie-breaking rule everyone accepts: lower stays lower. The rule crowns a unique king.
One small honesty note for the reverse direction: turning data back into ranks needs care when many data points tie (repeated values); ties must be broken with a coin flip. Generation — ranks into data — never has this problem.

You can watch this trick operating in the course demo Sampling as a Map, and it is the exact mechanism behind the two-point generator of W01. In one dimension, generative modeling is finished — a lookup in a percentile table.

title: Moving Distributions: The Transport Story
section: And in two dimensions, the trick dies
text:
And in two dimensions, the trick dies
Now let the data be pairs — a height and a weight; an image with many pixels. Try the rank trick: “what fraction of the data lies below this point?”
Below? Point A is up and to the left of point B. Which one is “lower”? In a plane there is no natural order. No order, no ranks; no ranks, no percentiles; no percentiles, no inverse CDF. The one canonical tool we had does not survive the second dimension.
Worse — the problem is not that transport becomes impossible. It becomes embarrassingly possible. Picture moving a round cloud of sand onto another round cloud: you can slide it straight over; or slide it over and rotate it by any angle; or swirl the middle while fixing the edge. Infinitely many transports do the job, and no one of them is the boss. In one dimension the never-cross rule crowned a unique king; in two dimensions there is no throne.
This is the honest statement of the difficulty: in higher dimensions, transport is not undefined — it is underdetermined. And the thing that is missing is precisely the tie-breaker: the line’s “lower stays lower” rule has no natural analogue in the plane. Something must be added to pick one map out of the infinite crowd.

title: Moving Distributions: The Transport Story
section: Every model family is a different way of choosing
text:
Every model family is a different way of choosing
Here is the reveal: the famous generative model families are exactly the famous ways of adding that missing choice.
Sort by coordinates anyway — normalizing flows. Alphabetical order: sort by the first coordinate; break ties with the second; and so on. This resurrects ranks, one coordinate at a time — transform the first coordinate by its percentiles, then the second given the first, and so on. It works at every scale, and it is exactly what autoregressive normalizing flows do. The cost: the answer depends on which coordinate you called “first,” as alphabetical order depends on the alphabet.
Move at the cheapest total cost — optimal transport. Charge for distance: among all valid transports, take the one minimizing the total moving bill. A deep theorem says that (in the natural settings) this again produces a unique map. The cost: computing it at scale is hard, and — a genuine surprise below — it is not what the popular generators actually compute.
Melt, then re-freeze — diffusion models. Refuse the direct matching entirely. Instead, melt the data — add noise a little at a time until every shape becomes the same formless Gaussian blob — and learn to run the melting backwards. Freezing is guided by a purely local question: “from here, which direction looks denser?” That local question is learnable by a neural network even in a million dimensions. Two choices select the route: the melting schedule, and — a subtlety — a no-swirling rule: many wind patterns produce the same evolution of the sand’s density (add any swirl that circulates without piling anything up), and diffusion picks the swirl-free wind. This is the entire subject of this course, met from a new side.
Fool the inspector — GANs. Train a forger against a detective: any transport whose output the detective cannot distinguish from data is accepted. Note what is missing: any transport. Here is how loose that is, even in one dimension: take the fair rank-matcher, but first fold the lottery ticket — send every rank \(u\) to \(1-u\), or crease it in the middle like a tent. The folded generator produces exactly the same distribution, so no inspector, however perfect, can object — yet it is not the rank map. GANs add no selection principle at all, which is part of why they are powerful and part of why they are temperamental.
Compress and decompress — VAEs. Learn an encoder that squeezes data into tidy randomness and a decoder that reinflates it. Here is a lovely secret: in one dimension, the perfect encoder is precisely the rank trick — the CDF! — and the perfect decoder is the inverse CDF. But two honest footnotes. First, nothing in the VAE’s training forces that choice: many equally good codes exist (swap all ranks \(u \leftrightarrow 1-u\), for a start), and the VAE has no reason to prefer the tidy one. Second, a textbook VAE is not even allowed to be perfectly tidy — its rules require the code to stay a little blurry (a perfectly sharp code costs it an infinite penalty). The “encoder = CDF” story is the idealized, noise-free, never-crossing limit of a VAE — a beautiful limit, and one the actual training objective does not select. The VAE illustrates underdeterminacy from the inside.

title: Moving Distributions: The Transport Story
section: The punchline: five roads, one destination — in 1-D only
text:
The punchline: five roads, one destination — in 1-D only
Run all five families on one-dimensional data, each trained to perfection and each given the natural tie-breaking rule (never cross), and they collapse into the same map: the rank trick. But the fine print matters, and it splits three ways. For the smooth-flow families — diffusion’s deterministic sampler, normalizing flows, flow matching — the collapse is a theorem: a one-dimensional flow physically cannot cross itself, so the tie-breaker comes built in (this course proves the diffusion case in The Deterministic Map, Proved). For GANs and VAEs the collapse is merely available: their training rules accept the rank map but do not prefer it — the folded forger and the blurry code are equally welcome. In one dimension the five philosophies can be one philosophy; only some of them insist on it.
In two dimensions and up, they genuinely part ways — and that is not a defect but the point: each family is one answer to a question that no longer has a single answer. If you understand (a) the 1-D trick, (b) why it dies upstairs, and (c) what each family adds to revive it, you understand the map of the whole field.

title: Moving Distributions: The Transport Story
section: A warning label: what not to carry upstairs
text:
A warning label: what not to carry upstairs
The 1-D picture is a superb ladder and a treacherous railing. Keep the ladder, do not lean on it:

“Lower stays lower” means nothing upstairs. There is no single order to preserve — and “monotone” does not become meaningless, it becomes many different things (several inequivalent notions replace it, and different fixes pick different ones).
“The transport” is not a phrase you may use without saying which selection rule you chose.
The diffusion route is not the cheapest route. In 1-D the melter and the cheapest mover coincide; in higher dimensions they provably differ — professionals conjectured otherwise in print and were corrected by a counterexample.
Even the melting does not determine the route by itself. Upstairs, many winds produce the same density evolution (swirls circulate without piling); the no-swirl rule is an extra choice, invisible in 1-D where there is no room to swirl.
Percentile bookkeeping is a 1-D luxury. The beautiful fact that a diffusing particle “rides its quantile” (proved in this course) has no higher-dimensional analogue.

title: Moving Distributions: The Transport Story
text:
Where to go from here
The rigorous twin of this tutorial — Generative Models as Transport: History and Validation — replays this story with theorems, dates, and citations: who proved the rank trick unique, who invented each fix and when, what exactly is true about the “VAE encoder = CDF” slogan, and where the counterexamples live. And the rest of the course is the deep dive into one of the five roads — the melt-and-refreeze road — chosen because its local, learnable steering question scales to the dimensions where images and language live.

title: Generative AI, in Its Simplest Form
text:
View 1: conditional generation (a hierarchical model)
The simplest latent-variable model:
\[
\mathbb{P}(z = 1) = \pi, \quad \mathbb{P}(z = 2) = 1 - \pi, \qquad
x \mid z \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(\mu_z,\, \sigma^2).
\]
Ancestral sampling generates by following the arrows: draw the latent coin \(z\), then draw \(x\) from the selected component. The observed marginal is obtained by summing out the latent:
\[
p(x) \;=\; \sum_{z} p(z)\, p(x \mid z)
\;=\; \pi\, \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_1, \sigma^2) + (1-\pi)\, \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_2, \sigma^2)
\]
— exactly the two-component mixture from the playground. A mixture is not just a formula; it is a generative story: population \(\to\) subpopulation \(\to\) individual.
Inference is the same hierarchy, run backwards. Given an observed \(x\), Bayes’ rule gives the posterior over the hidden coin:
\[
\mathbb{P}(z = 1 \mid x)
= \frac{\pi\, \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_1, \sigma^2)}
       {\pi\, \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_1, \sigma^2) + (1-\pi)\, \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_2, \sigma^2)} .
\]
For \(\mu_{1,2} = \mp 1\) and \(\pi = \tfrac12\) this equals \(\operatorname{sigmoid}(-2x/\sigma^2)\); its companion \(\mathbb{P}(z = 2 \mid x) = \operatorname{sigmoid}(2x/\sigma^2)\) is exactly the posterior W01 computed for the \(+1\) component, and the posterior mean of \(\mu_z\) is the tanh denoiser: W01’s denoising step was latent-variable inference all along. Generation and inference are the two directions of one arrow.

title: Generative AI, in Its Simplest Form
section: View 2: the coin disappears into a map
text:
View 2: the coin disappears into a map
Theorem (inverse-CDF / probability integral transform). Let \(F\) be a CDF with generalized inverse \(F^{-1}(u) = \inf\{x : F(x) \ge u\}\), and let \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\). Then \(X = F^{-1}(U)\) has CDF \(F\).
Proof. \(\mathbb{P}(F^{-1}(U) \le x) = \mathbb{P}(U \le F(x)) = F(x)\), since \(F^{-1}(u) \le x \iff u \le F(x)\) by monotonicity. \(\square\)
For our mixture, \(F(x) = \pi\,\Phi\!\big(\tfrac{x-\mu_1}{\sigma}\big) +
(1-\pi)\,\Phi\!\big(\tfrac{x-\mu_2}{\sigma}\big)\) is continuous and strictly increasing, so \(F^{-1}\) is an honest function, and
\[
u \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1), \qquad x = F^{-1}(u)
\]
generates the mixture with no coin anywhere — the explicit coin has been marginalized out. One caution about where it went: under this map, the event \(u < \pi\) selects the lowest \(\pi\)-fraction of the mixture distribution, which is not the same as the ancestral label \(z = 1\) when the components overlap — both Gaussians have full support, so each contributes on both sides of any quantile. (In the well-separated limit \(\sigma \to 0\) the two events do coincide, and the packed map below is the construction in which \(u < \pi\) genuinely encodes the coin.) Randomness in, structure out, everything in between deterministic.

title: Generative AI, in Its Simplest Form
text:
The two-point limit
Send \(\sigma \to 0\) with \(\mu_{1,2} = \mp 1\). The CDF collapses to a staircase: a jump of height \(\pi\) at \(-1\), a flat plateau at height \(\pi\) across the empty middle, a jump to \(1\) at \(+1\). The map becomes
\[
x = \begin{cases} -1, & u < \pi \\ +1, & u > \pi \end{cases}
\qquad\text{i.e.}\quad x = \operatorname{sign}(u - \pi),
\]
W01’s dataset, generated by thresholding a uniform (almost surely: the single point \(u = \pi\) has probability zero). The plateau is the geometric image of the empty region: no value of \(u\) lands there. The Deterministic Map, Proved proves this limit. (In the demo, slide \(\sigma\) down and watch the staircase form.)
crumbs: Generative AI, in Its Simplest Form

title: Generative AI, in Its Simplest Form
text:
Maps are not unique
\(F^{-1}\) is the monotone map pushing \(\text{Uniform}(0,1)\) to \(p\), but not the only map. The “packed” two-stage construction
\[
x = \begin{cases}
\mu_1 + \sigma\, \Phi^{-1}\!\big(u/\pi\big), & u < \pi,\\[2pt]
\mu_2 + \sigma\, \Phi^{-1}\!\big(\tfrac{u-\pi}{1-\pi}\big), & u \ge \pi,
\end{cases}
\]
also pushes uniform to the mixture (each branch rescales its segment of \([0,1]\) back to a full uniform — Exercise 3), and it is literally ancestral sampling written as one formula. Different map, same distribution: what is canonical is the distribution, not the transport. (In higher dimensions, choosing among the many maps is its own subject — optimal transport — which we will brush against later.)

sample \(p_\theta(x \mid z)\), i.e. \(T_\theta(z, \varepsilon)\)
ELBO / variational learning


Normalizing flow
\(z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\)
invertible \(f_\theta(z)\)

Diffusion
\(x_T \sim \mathcal{N}\); step noise if stochastic

The outer skeleton is shared — simple randomness, a sampling mechanism, data — while the learned object, the structural constraints, and the sampler differ. For diffusion in particular, determinism is a sampler choice: the probability-flow ODE is a deterministic map from \(x_T\); the reverse SDE consumes fresh noise at every step and is a deterministic function only of \((x_T, \text{all step noises})\).
In one dimension with a known CDF, the map is a formula. For images, the population law is unknown and no tractable multivariate inverse-CDF construction exists — so deep generative models learn a transport, density, score, or other ingredient of a sampler rather than writing the map down. And you have already run one: W01’s probability-flow ODE numerically transported a moment-matched Gaussian to within \(\approx \sigma_{\min}\) of the two-point data (W01 lists the approximations involved); with the exact terminal law, score, and integration, it is an exact deterministic transport — an inverse-CDF-like map built not from the CDF but from the score, which is exactly the object a neural network can learn in high dimension. That construction, done properly, is Modules 4–6.

title: The World’s Smallest Diffusion Model
text:
The dataset
Our data distribution puts equal mass on two points:
\[
p_{\text{data}}(x_0) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\,\delta(x_0 + 1) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\,\delta(x_0 - 1),
\qquad x_0 \in \{-1, +1\}.
\]
Generative modeling asks: given samples from \(p_{\text{data}}\), produce more samples. For this dataset the answer is a coin flip — which is exactly why it is the right dataset: the machinery becomes transparent.

title: The World’s Smallest Diffusion Model
section: Forward process: noise melts the data
text:
Forward process: noise melts the data
Corrupt a clean sample with Gaussian noise of size \(\sigma\):
\[
x_\sigma \;=\; x_0 + \sigma z, \qquad z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1) \text{ independent of } x_0.
\]
Since \(x_0 = \pm 1\) with probability \(\tfrac12\) each, the density of the corrupted sample is a two-component Gaussian mixture:
\[
p_\sigma(x) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{N}(x;\, -1,\, \sigma^2)
\;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{N}(x;\, +1,\, \sigma^2).
\]
Two facts, both visible in the demo:

Small \(\sigma\): two sharp bumps at \(\pm 1\) — the data is intact.
Large \(\sigma\): the bumps merge. Indeed \(\mathbb{E}[x_\sigma] = 0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(x_\sigma) = \mathbb{E}[x_0^2] + \sigma^2 = 1 + \sigma^2\), and for \(\sigma \gtrsim 3\) the mixture is indistinguishable in practice from \(\mathcal{N}(0,\, 1 + \sigma^2)\) — at \(\sigma = 3\) its excess kurtosis is only \(-0.02\). (It is never exactly Gaussian at finite \(\sigma\); the precise statement is \(x_\sigma / \sqrt{1+\sigma^2} \Rightarrow \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) as \(\sigma \to \infty\).)

This is the first design principle of diffusion models: destroying structure is easy, fully understood, and ends somewhere known (a Gaussian), no matter what the data was.

title: The World’s Smallest Diffusion Model
section: Denoising: Bayes’ rule gives the optimal denoiser in closed form
text:
Denoising: Bayes’ rule gives the optimal denoiser in closed form
Now invert: we observe a noisy \(x_\sigma = x\) and want the clean \(x_0\). The best guess under squared error is the posterior mean \(\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_\sigma = x]\) (we will prove this optimality claim in Module 1; for now, take it).
The posterior over the two candidates follows from Bayes’ rule:
\[
\mathbb{P}(x_0 = +1 \mid x)
= \frac{\tfrac12\,\mathcal{N}(x; +1, \sigma^2)}
       {\tfrac12\,\mathcal{N}(x; +1, \sigma^2) + \tfrac12\,\mathcal{N}(x; -1, \sigma^2)}
= \frac{1}{1 + \exp\!\big(-\tfrac{2x}{\sigma^2}\big)}
= \operatorname{sigmoid}\!\Big(\frac{2x}{\sigma^2}\Big),
\]
where the middle step divides through by \(\mathcal{N}(x; +1, \sigma^2)\) and uses \(\exp\!\big(-\tfrac{(x+1)^2}{2\sigma^2}\big) \big/ \exp\!\big(-\tfrac{(x-1)^2}{2\sigma^2}\big)
= \exp\!\big(-\tfrac{2x}{\sigma^2}\big)\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{\;\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_\sigma = x]
= (+1)\,\mathbb{P}(+1 \mid x) + (-1)\,\mathbb{P}(-1 \mid x)
= \tanh\!\Big(\frac{x}{\sigma^2}\Big).\;}
\]
The optimal denoiser is a tanh — an activation function you already know, produced by nothing but probability. Sanity-check its two regimes:

\(\sigma \to 0\): \(\tanh(x/\sigma^2)\) becomes a hard step — snap to the nearer data point.
\(\sigma \to \infty\): \(\tanh(x/\sigma^2) \approx x/\sigma^2 \to 0\) — the observation is all noise, so the best guess is the prior mean \(0\).

title: The World’s Smallest Diffusion Model
section: The score function (a preview of Module 4)
text:
The score function (a preview of Module 4)
Differentiate \(\log p_\sigma\) directly. With \(\varphi_\pm(x) = \mathcal{N}(x; \pm 1, \sigma^2)\) and \(\varphi_\pm'(x) = -\tfrac{x \mp 1}{\sigma^2}\varphi_\pm(x)\),
\[
\nabla_x \log p_\sigma(x)
= \frac{\tfrac12\varphi_-'(x) + \tfrac12\varphi_+'(x)}{p_\sigma(x)}
= -\frac{x - \mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x]}{\sigma^2}
= \frac{\tanh\!\big(\tfrac{x}{\sigma^2}\big) - x}{\sigma^2}.
\]
Rearranged, this is Tweedie’s formula, one of the two or three most important identities of the course:
\[
\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_\sigma = x] \;=\; x + \sigma^2\, \nabla_x \log p_\sigma(x).
\]
Denoising and knowing the score are the same thing — for additive Gaussian noise of known size \(\sigma\), which is exactly the diffusion setting. The score \(\nabla_x \log p_\sigma\) points from \(x\) toward where the (noised) data is denser; the denoiser just moves by \(\sigma^2\) times the score. One caveat: the score is a local quantity — at \(x = 0\) it vanishes by symmetry even though, in the two-bump regime, \(x = 0\) is a density minimum. It is an unstable equilibrium: the reverse dynamics leave a particle sitting exactly there alone, and push a particle on either side away toward the nearer mode.

title: The World’s Smallest Diffusion Model
section: Reverse process: run the diffusion backwards
text:
Reverse process: run the diffusion backwards
Generation now works by annealing: start from pure noise at a large \(\sigma_{\max}\), and lower \(\sigma\) along a grid \(\sigma_{\max} = \sigma_0 > \sigma_1 > \cdots > \sigma_K \approx 0\), nudging the sample along the score at every step. (We write \(y_k\) for the reverse iterate at noise level \(\sigma_k\), keeping \(x_0\) reserved for the clean data point; \(y_0\) is pure noise and \(y_K\) is the generated sample.)
\[
y_{k+1} \;=\; y_k \;+\; \frac{\sigma_k^2 - \sigma_{k+1}^2}{2}\,
\nabla_y \log p_{\sigma_k}(y_k)
\;=\; y_k + \frac{\sigma_k^2 - \sigma_{k+1}^2}{2}\cdot
\frac{\tanh\!\big(y_k/\sigma_k^2\big) - y_k}{\sigma_k^2}.
\]
This deterministic rule is the explicit Euler discretization of the probability-flow ODE in the variance clock \(\tau = \sigma^2\). (Strictly, to speak of dynamics across noise levels we couple them: \(x_\tau = x_0 + w_\tau\) with \(w\) a Brownian motion — Module 5 makes this precise; nothing below needs it yet.) The stochastic variant both doubles the score drift and injects fresh independent noise at each step,
\[
y_{k+1} = y_k + \big(\sigma_k^2 - \sigma_{k+1}^2\big)\,\nabla_y \log p_{\sigma_k}(y_k)
+ \sqrt{\sigma_k^2 - \sigma_{k+1}^2}\; z_k, \qquad z_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)
\text{ i.i.d.},
\]
giving the Euler–Maruyama discretization of the reverse-time SDE. Where these updates come from is the business of Modules 5–6 (Fokker–Planck, reverse-time dynamics); today we only need to watch them work: a cloud of particles started from \(\mathcal{N}(0,\, 1+\sigma_{\max}^2)\) splits, condenses, and lands within \(\approx \sigma_{\min}\) of \(\{-1, +1\}\), in equal proportions up to sampling error.
To be honest about the word “exact”: the formulas are exact, but the sampler carries four small approximations — we initialize from the moment-matched Gaussian rather than the true mixture \(p_{\sigma_{\max}}\) (indistinguishable at \(\sigma_{\max} = 3\), but not equal); we stop at \(\sigma_{\min} = 10^{-2} > 0\), so samples end a hair’s width from the atoms; the Euler steps discretize the flow; and any finite run has sampling noise. Each vanishes in the appropriate limit — and every one of them has a counterpart in real diffusion models.
The full sampler, with no neural network anywhere:
import numpy as np

def score(y, s2):                 # ∇ log p_σ(y), exact for the two-point data
    return (np.tanh(y / s2) - y) / s2

smax, smin, K, N = 3.0, 1e-2, 500, 100_000
sig = smax * (smin / smax) ** (np.arange(K + 1) / K)    # geometric σ grid
y = np.sqrt(1 + smax**2) * np.random.randn(N)           # start from pure noise

for k in range(K):                                       # probability-flow ODE
    d = sig[k]**2 - sig[k + 1]**2
    y += 0.5 * d * score(y, sig[k]**2)

err = np.abs(np.abs(y) - 1).max()      # worst distance to the nearest data point
print(err, (y > 0).mean())   # ≈ 0 and ≈ 0.5, up to σ_min + discretization + sampling

title: The World’s Smallest Diffusion Model
section: Why the course exists: what breaks for images
text:
Why the course exists: what breaks for images
Everything above was exact because the posterior mean had a formula. For images there is no usable one. (Exercise 4 gives a closed form for any finite training set — but a sampler built on it can only ever reproduce the training points; what we actually want is the posterior mean under the unknown population distribution.) Nor can it be tabulated: a \(64 \times 64\) RGB image lives in a space of \(256^{12288}\) configurations, and the data occupies a vanishingly thin filament of it (Module 1: the curse of dimensionality). The entire role of the neural network in a diffusion model is to approximate the map \((x, \sigma) \mapsto \mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x]\) — to be the tanh we can no longer derive. Every other ingredient of this note survives unchanged, and each becomes a module of the course:

Check that as \(\sigma \to \infty\) this tends to \(2\pi - 1\), the prior mean, and work out what happens in the degenerate cases \(\pi \in \{0, 1\}\) by taking limits.

\propto \exp\!\big(-\tfrac{(x - a_i)^2}{2\sigma^2}\big)\) — a softmax with Gaussian-kernel weights. (So the optimal denoiser for a finite dataset under Gaussian corruption is attention-like: an RBF-weighted average of the training points. For non-uniform weights \(\pi_i\), each logit gains \(\log \pi_i\).)

title: The Deterministic Map, Proved
text:
The claim, and the route
Fix \(\sigma > 0\) and consider the symmetric two-component Gaussian mixture with equal weights and means \(\pm 1\):
\[
p_\sigma(x) = \tfrac12\,\mathcal{N}(x; -1, \sigma^2) + \tfrac12\,\mathcal{N}(x; +1, \sigma^2),
\qquad
F_\sigma(x) = \tfrac12\,\Phi\!\Big(\frac{x+1}{\sigma}\Big) + \tfrac12\,\Phi\!\Big(\frac{x-1}{\sigma}\Big),
\]
where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal CDF. (Throughout, \(p_\sigma\) denotes both the density and its law; pushforwards act on the law.) Two statements are to be proved:
The route runs in five steps, each a plain claim backed by formal results: (1) sampling is a map — a uniform pushed through an inverse CDF acquires that CDF (Theorem 1); (2) our mixture admits the map — \(F_\sigma\) is a smooth bijection, so \(T_\sigma\) exists and is smooth (Proposition 2); (3) symmetry halves the work (Lemma 3); (4) a squeeze argument gives the sign-function limit (Theorem 4), with its distributional consequences (Corollary 5); (5) the fine structure — the shape of the stairs and the forming jump. Steps 1–5 build and analyze the one-shot map; the second half of the tutorial then earns the deeper claim — the score-driven reverse flow is the same map, and the practical sampler is its numerical solution. The theorems are the scaffolding; the argument is the building.

title: The Deterministic Map, Proved
text:
There exists a smooth, strictly increasing map \(T_\sigma\) with \(T_\sigma(U) \sim p_\sigma\) for \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\).
As \(\sigma \downarrow 0\), \(T_\sigma(u) \to \operatorname{sign}(u - \tfrac12)\) for every fixed \(u \in (0,1) \setminus \{\tfrac12\}\) — the generator of the two-point distribution \(\tfrac12\,\delta_{-1} + \tfrac12\,\delta_{+1}\), which is the \(\sigma \to 0\) limit of the mixture.

title: The Deterministic Map, Proved
text:
Step 1 — Sampling is a map
The entire construction rests on one line: a uniform random number pushed through an inverse CDF is a sample from that CDF. Stated exactly:
Theorem 1 (probability integral transform). Let \(F\) be a continuous, strictly increasing CDF mapping \(\mathbb{R}\) onto \((0,1)\), and let \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\). Then \(X = F^{-1}(U)\) has CDF \(F\).
Proof. Monotonicity of \(F\) gives the equivalence \(F^{-1}(u) \le x \iff u \le F(x)\). Hence
\[
\mathbb{P}\big(F^{-1}(U) \le x\big) = \mathbb{P}\big(U \le F(x)\big) = F(x). \qquad\square
\]
(For CDFs that are not strictly increasing or not continuous, the same conclusion holds with the generalized inverse \(F^{-1}(u) = \inf\{x : F(x) \ge u\}\); Exercise 1.)

title: The Deterministic Map, Proved
section: Step 2 — The mixture admits the map
text:
Step 2 — The mixture admits the map
Step 1 applies to our target as soon as \(F_\sigma\) is invertible — and it is, smoothly, at every positive noise level. That is the whole content of the supporting result:
Proposition 2 (existence and smoothness). \(F_\sigma\) is a smooth, strictly increasing bijection of \(\mathbb{R}\) onto \((0,1)\). Consequently \(T_\sigma := F_\sigma^{-1}\) exists, is smooth, and satisfies
\[
T_\sigma'(u) \;=\; \frac{1}{p_\sigma\big(T_\sigma(u)\big)} \;>\; 0 .
\]
Proof. \(F_\sigma' = p_\sigma\), which is everywhere positive; hence \(F_\sigma\) is strictly increasing. Both \(\Phi\) terms tend to \(0\) as \(x \to -\infty\) and to \(1\) as \(x \to +\infty\), so \(F_\sigma\) maps onto \((0,1)\) and is a bijection. Smoothness of \(T_\sigma\) and the derivative formula follow from the inverse function theorem. \(\square\)
The derivative formula deserves a comment, because it already contains the tutorial’s central picture. \(T_\sigma\) is steepest exactly where the density is smallest. Between the two bumps of \(p_\sigma\) the density is nearly zero, so \(F_\sigma\) is nearly flat there — a plateau at height \(\tfrac12\) — and its inverse is correspondingly near-vertical. As \(\sigma\) shrinks, the graph of \(T_\sigma\) therefore sharpens into a staircase: two long, nearly flat treads (inputs \(u < \tfrac12\) landing near \(-1\), inputs \(u > \tfrac12\) landing near \(+1\)) joined by an ever-steeper riser at \(u = \tfrac12\). The remaining steps make this picture exact: the treads flatten onto the values \(\pm 1\) (Step 4), and each tread retains a \(\sigma\)-sized microstructure (Step 5).

title: The Deterministic Map, Proved
text:
Step 3 — Symmetry halves the work
The target is symmetric about the origin, and its map inherits the symmetry: the map is odd about the center point \(u = \tfrac12\), so any limit statement proved on one side transfers to the other. The supporting computation:
Lemma 3 (symmetry). \(F_\sigma(-x) = 1 - F_\sigma(x)\) for all \(x\); consequently \(T_\sigma(1-u) = -T_\sigma(u)\) for all \(u \in (0,1)\), and \(T_\sigma(\tfrac12) = 0\).
Proof. Using \(\Phi(-t) = 1 - \Phi(t)\) on each term,
\[
F_\sigma(-x)
= \tfrac12\,\Phi\!\Big(\frac{1-x}{\sigma}\Big) + \tfrac12\,\Phi\!\Big(\frac{-1-x}{\sigma}\Big)
= \tfrac12\Big[1 - \Phi\!\Big(\frac{x-1}{\sigma}\Big)\Big]
+ \tfrac12\Big[1 - \Phi\!\Big(\frac{x+1}{\sigma}\Big)\Big]
= 1 - F_\sigma(x).
\]
Applying \(T_\sigma\) to both sides of \(F_\sigma(-x) = 1 - F_\sigma(x)\) with \(u = F_\sigma(x)\) yields \(T_\sigma(1-u) = -T_\sigma(u)\); setting \(u = \tfrac12\) gives \(T_\sigma(\tfrac12) = -T_\sigma(\tfrac12) = 0\). \(\square\)
By the lemma, it suffices to analyze \(u < \tfrac12\).

title: The Deterministic Map, Proved
section: Step 4 — In the limit, the map is the sign function
text:
Step 4 — In the limit, the map is the sign function
The idea is a squeeze: to show \(T_\sigma(u) \to -1\), trap \(T_\sigma(u)\) between \(-1 - \varepsilon\) and \(-1 + \varepsilon\) by evaluating \(F_\sigma\) at those two points and letting monotonicity do the rest. Two evaluations, one theorem.
Theorem 4 (the limit is the sign function). For every fixed \(u \in (0,1)\) with \(u \ne \tfrac12\),
\[
\lim_{\sigma \downarrow 0} T_\sigma(u) \;=\; \operatorname{sign}\big(u - \tfrac12\big).
\]
Proof. By Lemma 3 it suffices to treat \(u < \tfrac12\) and show \(T_\sigma(u) \to -1\). Fix \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\). Evaluate \(F_\sigma\) at the two points \(-1 \pm \varepsilon\) and let \(\sigma \downarrow 0\):
\[
F_\sigma(-1+\varepsilon)
= \tfrac12\,\Phi\!\Big(\frac{\varepsilon}{\sigma}\Big)
+ \tfrac12\,\Phi\!\Big(\frac{\varepsilon - 2}{\sigma}\Big)
\;\longrightarrow\; \tfrac12 \cdot 1 + \tfrac12 \cdot 0 = \tfrac12,
\]
since \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(\varepsilon - 2 < 0\). Because \(u < \tfrac12\), there is a \(\sigma_1 > 0\) with \(F_\sigma(-1+\varepsilon) > u\) for all \(\sigma < \sigma_1\); by strict monotonicity of \(F_\sigma\) this gives \(T_\sigma(u) < -1 + \varepsilon\). Similarly,
\[
F_\sigma(-1-\varepsilon)
= \tfrac12\,\Phi\!\Big(\frac{-\varepsilon}{\sigma}\Big)
+ \tfrac12\,\Phi\!\Big(\frac{-2-\varepsilon}{\sigma}\Big)
\;\longrightarrow\; 0,
\]
so there is a \(\sigma_2 > 0\) with \(F_\sigma(-1-\varepsilon) < u\) for \(\sigma < \sigma_2\), whence \(T_\sigma(u) > -1 - \varepsilon\). For \(\sigma < \min(\sigma_1, \sigma_2)\) we conclude \(|T_\sigma(u) - (-1)| < \varepsilon\). \(\square\)
At the single point \(u = \tfrac12\), Lemma 3 gives \(T_\sigma(\tfrac12) = 0\) for every \(\sigma\); since \(\mathbb{P}(U = \tfrac12) = 0\), this point is irrelevant to the distributional statement below.

Consequences: the discrete generator as a limit of smooth ones
Corollary 5 (modes of convergence). Let \(S(u) = \operatorname{sign}(u - \tfrac12)\). Theorem 4 states \(T_\sigma(U) \to S(U)\) almost surely. Almost-sure convergence implies convergence in distribution, and \(S(U)\) takes the values \(\pm 1\) with probability \(\tfrac12\) each; hence
\[
p_\sigma \;\Longrightarrow\; \tfrac12\,\delta_{-1} + \tfrac12\,\delta_{+1}
\qquad (\sigma \downarrow 0),
\]
recovering the two-point distribution \(\tfrac12\,\delta_{-1} +
\tfrac12\,\delta_{+1}\) as the weak limit of the mixtures. The discrete generator \(x = S(u)\) — thresholding a uniform — is thereby exhibited as the pointwise limit of smooth generators.

title: The Deterministic Map, Proved
section: Step 5 — The fine structure: how the stairs and the jump form
text:
Step 5 — The fine structure: how the stairs and the jump form
Two refinements sharpen the qualitative theorem.
The shape of each stair. Fix \(u < \tfrac12\) and write \(x = T_\sigma(u)\), which by Theorem 4 lies near \(-1\) for small \(\sigma\); in particular \(x \le 0\) eventually, so the far component satisfies \(0 < \tfrac12\Phi\big(\tfrac{x-1}{\sigma}\big) \le \tfrac12\Phi(-1/\sigma)\), exponentially small. From \(u = F_\sigma(x)\),
\[
\Phi\!\Big(\frac{x+1}{\sigma}\Big) = 2u - 2\eta_\sigma,
\qquad 0 < \eta_\sigma \le \tfrac12\,\Phi(-1/\sigma),
\]
and therefore
\[
T_\sigma(u) \;=\; -1 + \sigma\,\Phi^{-1}\!\big(2u - 2\eta_\sigma\big)
\;\approx\; -1 + \sigma\,\Phi^{-1}(2u).
\]
Each tread of the limiting staircase carries a copy of the Gaussian quantile function, compressed by the factor \(\sigma\) — asymptotically, the inverse-CDF map coincides with the two-stage sampler that first chooses the component from \(u\) (below or above \(\tfrac12\)) and then applies that component’s own Gaussian quantile.
The forming jump. At the center, Proposition 2 gives
\[
T_\sigma'(\tfrac12) = \frac{1}{p_\sigma(0)} = \sigma\sqrt{2\pi}\; e^{1/(2\sigma^2)}
\;\longrightarrow\; \infty ,
\]
so the slope at \(u = \tfrac12\) blows up as the jump forms. Convergence in Theorem 4 is uniform on compact subsets of \((0,1) \setminus \{\tfrac12\}\) (by uniform continuity of \(\Phi^{-1}\) on compact subintervals together with the uniform exponential bound on the far component) but not across \(u = \tfrac12\): a boundary layer of width shrinking with \(\sigma\) always remains — the same non-uniform sharpening by which the smooth function \(\tanh(x/\sigma^2)\) approaches \(\operatorname{sign}(x)\).

title: The Deterministic Map, Proved
section: The score-based flow is the same map
text:
The score-based flow is the same map
The objective. The first half of this tutorial constructed one generator: the quantile map \(T_\sigma\). This section confronts it with a second construction — the score-driven flow at the heart of diffusion models — built from entirely different ingredients, and settles their exact relationship. First, the problem both constructions solve, stated as a problem:

The one-shot transport problem. Given the source law \(p_{\sigma_{\max}}\) and the target law \(p_{\sigma_{\min}}\), find a deterministic map \(M\) such that if the input is distributed as \(p_{\sigma_{\max}}\), the output \(M(X)\) is distributed as \(p_{\sigma_{\min}}\) — in symbols, \(M_\# \, p_{\sigma_{\max}} = p_{\sigma_{\min}}\), where \(M_\# \mu\) denotes the pushforward: the law of \(M(X)\) when \(X \sim \mu\).

Definition (quantile transport). For laws \(\mu, \nu\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) with continuous, strictly increasing CDFs \(F_\mu, F_\nu\), the quantile transport from \(\mu\) to \(\nu\) is
\[
Q_{\mu \to \nu} \;:=\; F_\nu^{-1} \circ F_\mu .
\]
It solves the transport problem — \(F_\mu(X) \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\) for \(X \sim \mu\) (the probability integral transform read forward), and Theorem 1 then carries the uniform to \(\nu\) — and by Proposition 7 (proved below) it is the unique continuous, strictly increasing solution. It matches each \(\mu\)-quantile to the same \(\nu\)-quantile: median to median, 90th percentile to 90th percentile.
The one-shot solution to our problem is \(Q_{p_{\sigma_{\max}} \to\, p_{\sigma_{\min}}} = F_{\sigma_{\min}}^{-1} \circ
F_{\sigma_{\max}}\): one formula, evaluated in a single stroke. The incremental solution flows particles down the noise ladder along the score of the current level. Two functions describe that local geometry. The posterior-mean denoiser
\[
D_\sigma(x) := \mathbb{E}[X_0 \mid X_\sigma = x] = \tanh(x/\sigma^2)
\]
is the conditional mean of the clean point given a noisy observation — the quantity diffusion models learn — and the score is its rescaled displacement,
\[
s_\sigma(x) = \partial_x \log p_\sigma(x)
= \frac{D_\sigma(x) - x}{\sigma^2}
\]
(differentiate \(\log p_\sigma\) to check). One caution about the resulting motion: it is not always “toward the nearer bump”. At high noise (\(\sigma > 1\)) the reverse field contracts everything toward the center; only once \(\sigma\) drops below \(1\) does the origin destabilize and the two clusters separate — the stability computation appears at the end of Layer 1. On the surface the two constructions look like different algorithms that happen to share endpoints. The claim — stated first, then earned in three layers — is much stronger.
Before any claims, two conventions and a cast of characters. Clock: \(\tau = \sigma^2\) is the variance clock; for \(\tau\)-indexed objects we write \(\bar p_\tau := p_{\sqrt{\tau}}\), \(\bar F_\tau := F_{\sqrt{\tau}}\), and \(\bar s_\tau := \partial_x \log \bar p_\tau\), so that subscripts never silently change meaning. Ladder: \(\sigma_{\max} = \sigma_0 > \sigma_1 >
\cdots > \sigma_K = \sigma_{\min}\) denotes a descending sequence of noise levels (fixed when Layer 3 needs it; until then \(\Psi_{a \to b}\) makes sense for any two levels \(a > b\)). Five distinct objects appear in this section, and they are easy to blur into one another:








Object
Symbol
What kind of thing it is




score
\(s_\sigma(x) = \partial_x \log p_\sigma(x)\)
a function of position, one per noise level — the local steering information; for our mixture, \((\tanh(x/\sigma^2) - x)/\sigma^2\)


velocity field
\(v = -\tfrac12\, \bar s_\tau\) (variance clock)
an arrow attached to every (position, level) pair — built from the score; the sampler traverses it toward smaller \(\tau\)


the flow (ODE)
\(dx/d\tau = v(x, \tau)\)
a dynamical rule: from a starting point, integrate to get a trajectory


flow map
\(\Psi_{a \to b}\)
a function \(\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\): feed in a position at level \(a\), integrate the ODE down to level \(b\), read off where the trajectory ends


pushforward
\(\Psi_\# \mu\)
not a new object but an operation: the law of the outputs when the inputs have law \(\mu\)



So \(\Psi_{\sigma_0 \to \sigma_K}\) is not the score, and not a measure: it is the deterministic input–output function obtained by integrating the score-built velocity field from level \(\sigma_0\) down to \(\sigma_K\); \(\Psi_{\sigma_k \to \sigma_{k+1}}\) is the same construction run over a single leg. The pushforward is how any map — this one included — acts on distributions, and the sentence “the flow solves the transport problem” means exactly \(\Psi_\#\, p_{\sigma_{\max}} =
p_{\sigma_{\min}}\): it is a candidate \(M\) for the transport problem stated above.






Key takeaway



They are one and the same solution, at three levels of resolution. (i) Identity: in one dimension the exact probability-flow map is the quantile transport \(F_{\sigma_{\min}}^{-1} \circ F_{\sigma_{\max}}\) — at every positive noise level, not only in a limit. (ii) Mechanism: the flow conserves the quantile: \(u = \bar F_\tau(x_\tau)\) is constant along every trajectory, so the one-shot map jumps each point to its quantile’s final position while the flow tracks the same quantile continuously through every intermediate law. (iii) Consequence: every adjacent pair of noise levels admits its own quantile transport; each step of the practical sampler is the first-order approximation of that per-step quantile map; and the telescoping identity composes the per-step maps back into the one-shot transport — so reverse diffusion is, literally, a numerical solution of the one-shot transport problem.


The layers prove, in order: the flow map equals the quantile transport \(Q\) (Layer 1); the reason is that it conserves quantiles (Layer 2); and it factorizes leg by leg, with the sampler as its Euler discretization (Layer 3).
The descent, in one chain. The whole section — many-step reverse diffusion down to the one-shot inverse CDF — is the following sequence of constructions and identifications, each arrow one step:
\[
\begin{gathered}
\text{score } s_\sigma = \partial_x \log p_\sigma \\[-1pt]
\big\downarrow \; {\scriptstyle \text{scale}} \\[-1pt]
\text{velocity field } v = -\tfrac12\, \bar s_\tau \\[-1pt]
\big\downarrow \; {\scriptstyle \text{impose as dynamics}} \\[-1pt]
\text{ODE } \; dx/d\tau = v(x, \tau) \\[-1pt]
\big\downarrow \; {\scriptstyle \text{integrate — exactly: the flow; per frozen step: Euler, the } K\text{-step sampler}} \\[-1pt]
\text{flow map } \Psi_{\sigma_{\max} \to \sigma_{\min}} \\[-1pt]
\big\downarrow \; {\scriptstyle \text{pushforward } \Psi_\# p_{\sigma_{\max}} = p_{\sigma_{\min}} \;+\; \text{monotone (no crossing)} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{rigidity}} \\[-1pt]
\text{quantile transport } Q = F_{\sigma_{\min}}^{-1} \circ F_{\sigma_{\max}}
\quad {\scriptstyle \text{(each leg identified by rigidity; legs composed by telescoping)}} \\[-1pt]
\big\downarrow \; {\scriptstyle \sigma_{\min} \downarrow 0} \\[-1pt]
\operatorname{sign}(x) \;\; {\scriptstyle \text{(the two-point generator)}}
\end{gathered}
\]
Read downward, the chain is how reverse diffusion is built; the pushforward-plus-monotonicity arrow is where it is identified with the one-shot map — note that the pushforward property alone would not suffice (many maps carry \(p_{\sigma_{\max}}\) to \(p_{\sigma_{\min}}\)); it is pushforward together with monotonicity that forces \(\Psi = Q\), by Proposition 7. Everything below is this chain, one arrow at a time.

Layer 1 — the identity
(premise) — the flow transports the family. Everything below uses one fact about the flow: it reproduces the prescribed marginals, \((\Psi_{a \to b})_\#\, p_a = p_b\). This is the defining property of the probability-flow field, verified by one rearrangement: with \(v = -\tfrac12\, \bar s_\tau\) we have \(\bar p_\tau v = -\tfrac12\, \partial_x \bar p_\tau\), so the continuity equation \(\partial_\tau \bar p_\tau + \partial_x(\bar p_\tau v) = 0\) is exactly the heat equation \(\partial_\tau \bar p_\tau = \tfrac12\, \partial_x^2 \bar p_\tau\), which the Gaussian-mixture family satisfies (the componentwise check opens Layer 2). An ensemble started with law \(p_a\) and moved by the ODE therefore arrives with law \(p_b\); Layer 2 sharpens this ensemble statement to a particlewise conservation law.
(a) — flows cannot cross, so the flow map is monotone.
Proposition 6 (flows do not cross). For \(\sigma_{\min} > 0\), let \(\Psi\) denote the exact probability-flow ODE map carrying noise level \(\sigma_{\max}\) down to \(\sigma_{\min}\) (the field \(v = -\tfrac12\, \bar s_\tau\), integrated toward smaller \(\tau\), exact score). Then \(\Psi\) is continuous and strictly increasing.
Proof sketch. The field is smooth, and its spatial derivative is globally bounded on the band: \(s_\sigma'(x) = \sigma^{-4}\operatorname{sech}^2(x/\sigma^2)
- \sigma^{-2}\) is bounded uniformly for \(\sigma \in [\sigma_{\min},
\sigma_{\max}]\), so solutions exist across the whole leg and are unique. If two trajectories starting at \(x < x'\) met at some time, running the ODE backwards from the meeting point would violate uniqueness; hence trajectories preserve order, and \(\Psi\) is strictly increasing. Continuity of the flow map in the initial condition is standard ODE theory. \(\square\)
(b) — a monotone transport between two given laws is unique.
Proposition 7 (monotone transport is rigid). Let \(T\) be continuous and strictly increasing with \(T_\# \mu = \nu\), where \(\mu, \nu\) have continuous, strictly increasing CDFs \(F_\mu, F_\nu\). Then \(T = F_\nu^{-1} \circ F_\mu\).
Proof. \(F_\nu(T(x)) = \nu\big((-\infty, T(x)]\big)
= \mu\big(T^{-1}(-\infty, T(x)]\big) = \mu\big((-\infty, x]\big) = F_\mu(x)\), using monotonicity in the middle step. Apply \(F_\nu^{-1}\). \(\square\)
(c) — identify the flow, then take the limit.
Corollary 8. The end-to-end flow map satisfies \(\Psi_{\sigma_{\max} \to \sigma_{\min}} = F_{\sigma_{\min}}^{-1} \circ
F_{\sigma_{\max}}\): the flow map of the probability-flow ODE is the quantile transport, at every positive noise level. Composing with a uniform parametrization of the source — write \(x_T\) for a starting position at the top level, \(x_T = F_{\sigma_{\max}}^{-1}(u)\) — the composite \(u \mapsto \Psi\big(F_{\sigma_{\max}}^{-1}(u)\big)\) is exactly the map \(T_{\sigma_{\min}}\) of Step 2: uniform noise in, mixture sample out, through the flow. Theorem 4 therefore applies verbatim: as \(\sigma_{\min} \downarrow 0\),
\[
\Psi(x_T) \;\longrightarrow\; \operatorname{sign}(x_T)
\qquad \text{for every } x_T \ne 0,
\]
since \(F_{\sigma_{\max}}(0) = \tfrac12\) by symmetry. The tanh-driven flow converges pointwise to the deterministic two-point generator. Its separatrix \(x_T = 0\) — where the score vanishes by symmetry — is an equilibrium of the reverse dynamics whose character changes with the noise level: since \(\tfrac12 s_\sigma'(0) = \tfrac12(\sigma^{-4} - \sigma^{-2})\), the origin attracts while \(\sigma > 1\), is neutral at \(\sigma = 1\), and repels once \(\sigma < 1\) — the two regimes announced in the objective.
The identity, applied to the example. Corollary 8 is not only a structural fact — for this tutorial’s mixture it is a computable formula. Plugging the CDFs in:
\[
\Psi(x)
= F_{\sigma_{\min}}^{-1}\!\Big(
\tfrac12\, \Phi\big(\tfrac{x+1}{\sigma_{\max}}\big)
+ \tfrac12\, \Phi\big(\tfrac{x-1}{\sigma_{\max}}\big)
\Big).
\]
The outer inverse has no closed form (numerically, one bisects it) — but the stair asymptotics of Step 5, applied here to the transport itself for the first time, give a closed-form asymptotic for it. With \(u = F_{\sigma_{\max}}(x)\),
\[
\Psi(x) \;\approx\;
\begin{cases}
-1 + \sigma_{\min}\, \Phi^{-1}(2u), & u < \tfrac12,\\[2pt]
+1 + \sigma_{\min}\, \Phi^{-1}(2u - 1), & u > \tfrac12.
\end{cases}
\]
Read as a formula, the applied transport is a soft sign: to leading order it collapses every input to \(\pm 1\) — Theorem 4’s limit, now visible term by term — while the \(O(\sigma_{\min})\) residue records where within its cluster the sample lands: the conserved quantile, miniaturized into the stair. Concretely, for \(\sigma_{\max} = 3\), \(\sigma_{\min} = 10^{-2}\):
