Agreement to every displayed digit — and the exact column consists of the same numbers the ODE integration produces in the evidence paragraph below: one map, computed three independent ways (integrated flow, bisected quantile transport, stair asymptotics). The table also teaches how the map thinks: \(x = 1\) and \(x = 2\), though far apart, both land within \(10^{-2}\) of \(+1\) — the cluster forgets the details — while the extreme draw \(x = 6\) lands beyond the atom, at \(1.0158\), because its within-cluster quantile \(\Phi^{-1}(0.9424) \approx 1.58\) is carried, shrunk by \(\sigma_{\min}\), into the stair. The transport is \(\operatorname{sign}(x)\) plus quantile bookkeeping. And the transport problem that opened this section is now solved twice over, with the two solutions identified: \(M = Q = \Psi\).


Layer 2 — the mechanism: the flow conserves quantiles
The identity of Layer 1 is proved but not yet explained: why should an ODE driven by local score information reproduce a map built from global CDFs? The answer is a conservation law, and it takes two lines.
Work in the variance clock (\(\bar p_\tau, \bar F_\tau, \bar s_\tau\) as fixed in the conventions above). Each mixture component \(\mathcal{N}(x; \pm 1, \tau)\) is a heat kernel, so the family satisfies the heat equation \(\partial_\tau \bar p_\tau = \tfrac12 \partial_x^2 \bar p_\tau\) (differentiate a Gaussian once in \(\tau\) and twice in \(x\) to check; linearity does the rest). Integrating from \(-\infty\) to \(x\), using \(\partial_x \bar p_\tau \to 0\) at \(-\infty\), gives the CDF’s equation of motion:
\[
\partial_\tau \bar F_\tau(x) = \tfrac12\, \partial_x \bar p_\tau(x).
\]
Now let \(x(\tau)\) be any trajectory of the probability-flow ODE, \(\dot x = v(x, \tau) = -\tfrac12\, \bar s_\tau(x)\) (the reverse sampler traverses the same curves toward smaller \(\tau\) — reversed limits, same field). By the chain rule,
\[
\frac{d}{d\tau} \bar F_\tau\big(x(\tau)\big)
= \partial_\tau \bar F_\tau(x) + \bar p_\tau(x)\, \dot x
= \tfrac12\, \partial_x \bar p_\tau(x)
- \bar p_\tau(x) \cdot \tfrac12\, \partial_x \log \bar p_\tau(x)
= 0 .
\]
The quantile \(u = \bar F_\tau(x_\tau)\) is a conserved quantity of the flow. Three things follow at once.

Layer 1, re-derived in one line. A trajectory started at \(x_T\) carries \(u = F_{\sigma_{\max}}(x_T)\) unchanged, so it must terminate at \(F_{\sigma_{\min}}^{-1}(u)\) — Corollary 8 again, obtained now without the rigidity argument.
No-crossing, explained. Distinct trajectories carry distinct conserved quantiles, and \(\bar F_\tau\) is strictly increasing — so they can never meet. Proposition 6’s order-preservation is the shadow of a conservation law.







Trajectories are iso-quantile curves



For each fixed \(u \in (0,1)\), the level set \(\bar F_\tau(x) = u\) traces a smooth curve through the \((x, \tau)\) plane,
\[
\tau \;\longmapsto\; x_u(\tau) = \bar F_\tau^{-1}(u)
\]
— the iso-quantile curve of the evolving family: the locus of “the \(u\)-th quantile” as the noise level changes. The conservation law says exactly this: the flow’s trajectories are these curves. Every particle rides its own quantile line and never leaves it. And every map in this tutorial is a reading of this one bundle of curves:

the per-leg quantile transport \(Q_k\) reads one curve at two adjacent ladder levels;
the end-to-end flow map \(\Psi\) reads it at the top and bottom levels;
the one-shot map \(T_{\sigma_{\min}}\) parameterizes the curves by \(u\) itself and reads the bottom;
the staircase limit is the geometry of the whole bundle as \(\tau \downarrow 0\): every curve with \(u < \tfrac12\) funnels into \(-1\), every curve with \(u > \tfrac12\) funnels into \(+1\), and the single \(u = \tfrac12\) curve — the separatrix — stays pinned at \(0\).

One family of curves; the one-shot map, the flow, and the sampler are three ways of reading it — at the endpoint, continuously, and at ladder resolution.




Layer 3 — the factorization, and why “numerical solution” is literal
The conservation law upgrades naturally into an algebra of maps: three exact moves, followed by the Euler analysis.
Move 1 — at every step of the ladder, a quantile transport is available. Proposition 2 was stated at one fixed \(\sigma\), but its proof used nothing special about the level: every \(F_s\) with \(s > 0\) is a smooth, strictly increasing bijection onto \((0,1)\). Hence for each adjacent pair of the ladder \(\sigma_{\max} = \sigma_0 > \sigma_1 > \cdots > \sigma_K = \sigma_{\min}\), the per-step quantile transport
\[
Q_k \;:=\; Q_{p_{\sigma_k} \to\, p_{\sigma_{k+1}}} \;=\; F_{\sigma_{k+1}}^{-1} \circ F_{\sigma_k}
\]
is well-defined, and by Proposition 7 it is the unique monotone map carrying level \(\sigma_k\) to level \(\sigma_{k+1}\). The one-shot problem has been sliced into \(K\) sub-problems of the same kind, each with its own one-shot solution.
Move 2 — each leg of the exact flow is that per-step quantile transport. Layer 1’s argument applies verbatim on the sub-interval: the flow leg \(\Psi_{\sigma_k \to \sigma_{k+1}}\) is continuous and strictly increasing (no crossing) and pushes \(p_{\sigma_k}\) to \(p_{\sigma_{k+1}}\) (the flow reproduces the family), so by uniqueness \(\Psi_{\sigma_k \to \sigma_{k+1}} = Q_k\). Equivalently, by Layer 2: each leg carries every particle along its iso-quantile curve from one level to the next — quantile in, same quantile out.
Move 3 — telescoping identifies the composition with the one-shot map. Two independent derivations give the same identity. Dynamically, solution maps of an ODE compose — solving from \(\sigma_0\) down to \(\sigma_K\) while pausing at intermediate levels changes nothing, by uniqueness of solutions:
\[
\Psi_{\sigma_0 \to \sigma_K}
= \Psi_{\sigma_{K-1} \to \sigma_K} \circ \cdots \circ \Psi_{\sigma_0 \to \sigma_1}
= Q_{K-1} \circ \cdots \circ Q_0 .
\]
Analytically, the same chain is pure cancellation — each intermediate CDF annihilates its own inverse:
\[
\big(F_{\sigma_K}^{-1} \circ F_{\sigma_{K-1}}\big) \circ \cdots \circ
\big(F_{\sigma_1}^{-1} \circ F_{\sigma_0}\big)
= F_{\sigma_K}^{-1} \circ F_{\sigma_0}
= Q_{p_{\sigma_{\max}} \to\, p_{\sigma_{\min}}} .
\]
Together: the one-shot quantile transport factorizes exactly into per-level quantile transports. Nothing is approximate yet — the exact reverse flow is not an approximation of the one-shot map but a factorization of it.
The last move — connecting the exact factors to the practical sampler — is where “numerical solution” acquires its literal meaning, so it deserves a derivation rather than a remark.
Notation first. Re-index the ladder by the variance clock: \(\tau := \sigma^2\) and \(\tau_k := \sigma_k^2\), with \(\Delta_k := \tau_k - \tau_{k+1} > 0\) the length of the \(k\)-th leg. Then \(\Psi_{\tau_k \to \tau_{k+1}}\) denotes the same exact flow leg as \(\Psi_{\sigma_k \to \sigma_{k+1}}\) — one object, two indexings — and by Move 2 it equals the per-step quantile transport \(Q_k\).
The exact leg, in integral form. The probability-flow ODE is \(dx/d\tau = -\tfrac12\, \bar s_\tau(x)\); the sampler traverses it toward smaller \(\tau\), which reverses the limits of integration, not the sign of the field. Integrating one leg from \(\tau_k\) down to \(\tau_{k+1}\), started at \(x\):
\[
\Psi_{\tau_k \to \tau_{k+1}}(x)
= x + \int_{\tau_{k+1}}^{\tau_k}
\tfrac12\, \bar s_\tau\big(x(\tau)\big)\, d\tau ,
\]
where \(x(\tau)\) is the trajectory itself. This is exact — but not directly evaluable as written, because the integrand must be evaluated along the very trajectory being solved for.
The one approximation. Over a short leg, freeze the integrand at the leg’s known starting data \((x, \tau_k)\):
\[
\int_{\tau_{k+1}}^{\tau_k}
\tfrac12\, \bar s_\tau\big(x(\tau)\big)\, d\tau
= \frac{\Delta_k}{2}\, \bar s_{\tau_k}(x) \;+\; R_k(x).
\]
The frozen version defines the step map
\[
E_k(x) \;:=\; x + \frac{\Delta_k}{2}\, \bar s_{\tau_k}(x)
\]
— symbol for symbol, the reverse-diffusion sampler update. Freezing the velocity at the left endpoint of each step is the definition of the explicit Euler method, so the sampler is the Euler discretization of the reverse ODE by construction, not by analogy. The remainder is second order: fix a compact set \(C\) of starting points and a compact tube containing all exact trajectories from \(C\) (such a tube exists because the field’s spatial derivative is globally bounded on the band, as in Proposition 6), and let \(L\) bound the field’s derivatives on that tube. Along the leg the integrand then drifts by \(O(\Delta_k)\), and it is integrated over an interval of length \(\Delta_k\), so, uniformly on the tube,
\[
\big| E_k(x) - \Psi_{\tau_k \to \tau_{k+1}}(x) \big|
= |R_k(x)| \;\le\; \tfrac{L}{2}\, \Delta_k^2 .
\]
Read through Move 2, this inequality is the statement that each step of reverse diffusion is a per-level quantile transport, correct to first order: \(E_k = Q_k + O(\Delta_k^2)\).
From one step to the whole ladder. The sampler is the composition \(S_K := E_{K-1} \circ \cdots \circ E_0\); the exact transport is \(\Psi = Q_{K-1} \circ \cdots \circ Q_0\) (Move 3). Compare them by swapping one factor at a time. Write \(z_k := (Q_{k-1} \circ \cdots \circ Q_0)(x)\) for the exact state entering leg \(k\), and \(A_k := E_{K-1} \circ \cdots \circ E_{k+1}\) for the remaining Euler tail. Inserting the hybrid compositions and telescoping gives the pointwise identity
\[
S_K(x) - \Psi(x)
= \sum_{k=0}^{K-1}
\Big[ A_k\big(E_k(z_k)\big) - A_k\big(Q_k(z_k)\big) \Big]
\]
(nonlinear maps do not distribute over subtraction, so the difference must remain inside the tail \(A_k\)). Each \(E_j\) has derivative \(1 + \tfrac{\Delta_j}{2}\, \partial_x \bar s_{\tau_j}\), hence Lipschitz constant at most \(1 + L\Delta_j \le e^{L \Delta_j}\); every tail \(A_k\) is therefore Lipschitz with constant at most \(\Lambda := e^{L(\tau_{\max} - \tau_{\min})}\), independently of \(K\). Applying this to each bracket and then the local error bound \(|E_k(z_k) - Q_k(z_k)| \le \tfrac{L}{2}\Delta_k^2\),
\[
|S_K(x) - \Psi(x)|
\;\le\; \Lambda \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} \tfrac{L}{2}\, \Delta_k^2
\;\le\; \tfrac{\Lambda L}{2}\, (\tau_{\max} - \tau_{\min})\, \max_k \Delta_k
\]
which is \(O(1/K)\) for any quasi-uniform ladder (\(\max_k \Delta_k = O(1/K)\) in the variance clock). (The constants are finite for every \(\sigma_{\min} > 0\), though they grow as \(\sigma_{\min} \downarrow 0\) — the stiffness recorded under Scope.) Letting the mesh \(\max_k \Delta_k \to 0\):
\[
\boxed{\;
\lim_{\max_k \Delta_k \to 0}\; E_{K-1} \circ \cdots \circ E_0
\;=\; \Psi
\;=\; Q_{\,p_{\sigma_{\max}} \to\, p_{\sigma_{\min}}}
\;}
\]
uniformly on compact sets. The sampler and the one-shot map are not merely similar: the sampler converges to the one-shot map, at the Euler rate, and the derivation identifies every intermediate object along the way:
\[
\underbrace{F_{\sigma_{\min}}^{-1} \circ F_{\sigma_{\max}}}_{\text{one-shot solution}}
\;=\;
\underbrace{Q_{K-1} \circ \cdots \circ Q_0}_{\text{exact factorization (Move 3)}}
\;\approx\;
\underbrace{E_{K-1} \circ \cdots \circ E_0}_{\substack{\text{reverse diffusion: the sampler } S_K\\ \text{Euler, error } O(1/K)}}
\]
Reverse diffusion is a numerical solution of the one-shot transport problem in the same sense that Euler’s method is a numerical solution of an initial-value problem — because it is Euler’s method, applied to an ODE whose exact solution map is the one-shot transport. Not an analogy: an instance, now derived.
The evidence — testing all three clauses. Setup, fully specified: the ladder is geometric in \(\sigma\) (uniform in \(\log \sigma\)) with \(K = 20{,}000\) legs from \(\sigma_{\max} = 3\) to \(\sigma_{\min} = 10^{-2}\); the update is the derived \(E_k\); the starting grid is \(33\) equispaced points on \([-8, 8]\) with the near-separatrix points \(|x| < 0.25\) excluded (at \(x = 0\) both maps give \(0\) exactly, by symmetry; the numerical difficulty concentrates near the separatrix, where the stiffness peaks); errors are suprema over the grid. Results: \(\sup |S_K - Q| \approx 1.9 \times 10^{-5}\) — clause (i) and the Euler side of clause (iii), whose \(O(1/K)\) signature Exercise 8 has you measure. And clause (ii) tested directly: the conserved quantile \(\bar F_{\tau_k}(x_k)\), monitored along every trajectory, drifts from its initial value by at most \(9.8 \times 10^{-5}\) over all twenty thousand steps — an Euler-sized violation of an exact conservation law, exactly as the theory prescribes.
Why the incremental route is the one that scales. The factorization is also the interface between the mathematics and the learning. The one-shot map is globally wild — in the \(\sigma \to 0\) limit, discontinuous — and is built from the CDF, a global object unavailable in high dimension. Each Euler factor \(E_k\), by contrast, is near-identity and consumes only the score at a single noise level — a local quantity that is exactly a regression target (denoising); the exact factor \(Q_k\) would still need the two endpoint CDFs, so it is the Euler step, not the exact leg, that is purely local. A composition of many learnable maps realizes one unlearnable map. Structurally, this is a homotopy (continuation) method for sampling: embed the intractable target in a family \(\{p_\sigma\}\) terminating at an easy, approximately Gaussian high-noise law, and track the solution path — equivalently, by Layer 2, track each sample’s conserved quantile — one level at a time.
Scope. Two caveats frame the result. First, the identification of the flow with the quantile transport is special to one dimension, where “monotone” pins the transport down uniquely; in higher dimensions the probability-flow ODE defines a valid transport that is in general not the monotone (optimal-transport) map. Second, the statement concerns the exact score, exact terminal law, and exact integration; and the velocity field becomes increasingly stiff as \(\sigma_{\min} \downarrow 0\) — for this example the score’s derivative at the separatrix grows like \(\sigma^{-4}\) (compute: \(s'(0) = 1/\sigma^4 - 1/\sigma^2\)) — so the flow is smooth at every positive noise level even though its limit is discontinuous, which is the dynamical face of the boundary layer of Theorem 4.

title: The Deterministic Map, Proved
text:
Interpretation
The same step function has now appeared on both sides of the generative pipeline. In data space, the posterior-mean denoiser — the conditional mean \(\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x] = \tanh(x/\sigma^2)\) of the clean point given a noisy observation, the object diffusion models learn — sharpens into \(\operatorname{sign}(x)\). In noise space, the generator \(T_\sigma(u) \to \operatorname{sign}(u - \tfrac12)\). In both cases a smooth object degenerates into a discontinuous one precisely as the noise scale vanishes. This is the one-dimensional instance of a general phenomenon: discrete or lower-dimensional data distributions are reached as limits of smooth transports, and learnable models operate at small positive noise scales exactly because smooth maps can be represented and trained while their discontinuous limits cannot. Diffusion models anneal \(\sigma\) toward zero rather than starting there for this reason.

title: The Deterministic Map, Proved
text:
Exercises

Prove Theorem 1 for a general CDF \(F\) (not necessarily continuous or strictly increasing) using the generalized inverse \(F^{-1}(u) = \inf\{x : F(x) \ge u\}\).
Write out the case \(u > \tfrac12\) of Theorem 4 directly (without invoking Lemma 3), and verify that the two squeeze evaluations become \(F_\sigma(1-\varepsilon) \to \tfrac12\) and \(F_\sigma(1+\varepsilon) \to 1\).
Unequal weights. For the mixture \(\pi\,\mathcal{N}(-1,\sigma^2) + (1-\pi)\,\mathcal{N}(+1,\sigma^2)\) with \(0 < \pi < 1\), show \(T_\sigma(u) \to -1\) for \(u < \pi\) and \(T_\sigma(u) \to +1\) for \(u > \pi\): the location of the jump is the component weight.
Verify the derivative computation \(T_\sigma'(\tfrac12) = \sigma \sqrt{2\pi}\,
e^{1/(2\sigma^2)}\) and evaluate it numerically for \(\sigma = 0.5, 0.2, 0.1\).
Three components. For a symmetric three-component mixture with means \(-1, 0, +1\) and equal weights, describe the limit of \(T_\sigma\): the number of jumps, their locations in \(u\), and the limiting values between them.
Prove Proposition 7 in detail, identifying exactly where continuity and strict monotonicity of \(T\) are used.
Reproduce the numerical confirmation: integrate the exact-score probability-flow ODE with a fine step grid from a grid of initial points and compare with \(F_{\sigma_{\min}}^{-1} \circ F_{\sigma_{\max}}\) computed by bisection. Where is the agreement worst, and why?
The Euler signature. Rerun Exercise 7 with \(K = 25, 50, 100, 200, 400\) steps and plot the maximum deviation from the quantile transport against \(K\): confirm the \(O(1/K)\) decay predicted by the factorization argument. Additionally monitor \(\bar F_{\tau_k}(x_k)\) along each trajectory and check that its drift shrinks at the same rate — the direct test of quantile conservation.
Quantile conservation. (a) Verify that \(\mathcal{N}(x; \mu, \tau)\) satisfies the heat equation in the variance clock. (b) Re-derive \(\partial_\tau F_\tau = \tfrac12 \partial_x p_\tau\), stating the boundary behaviour used. (c) Prove the telescoping identity twice: by cancellation of CDFs, and by the pause-and-resume (semigroup) property of ODE solution maps.

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
The Probability-Flow ODE
text: A diffusion model learns a time-dependent velocity field that transports the (near-Gaussian) terminal law \(p_T\) of the forward process into the data distribution. Once the field is known, samples can be generated deterministically, by solving an ordinary differential equation.

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
text:
Two conventions: a dictionary
A warning before any formulas. The W01–W02 tutorials used the variance-exploding (VE) convention,
\[
x_\sigma = x_0 + \sigma z ,
\]
in which the clean signal is never rescaled and the variance grows without bound. This tutorial uses the variance-preserving (VP) convention standard in the DDPM literature, in which the signal is simultaneously attenuated:
\[
x_t = \alpha_t\, x_0 + \sigma_t\, \varepsilon,
\qquad \alpha_t^2 + \sigma_t^2 = 1 .
\]
The two are the same construction in different coordinates. The exact dictionary, valid whenever \(\alpha_t > 0\):
\[
\boxed{\;
\begin{aligned}
Y_t &= \frac{X_t}{\alpha_t} = X_0 + \tilde\sigma_t\, \varepsilon,
\qquad
\tilde\sigma_t^2 = \frac{\sigma_t^2}{\alpha_t^2} = \frac{1}{\alpha_t^2} - 1, \\[2pt]
s_Y(y, t) &= \alpha_t\, s_X(\alpha_t y,\, t)
\end{aligned}
\;}
\]
i.e. dividing the VP state by \(\alpha_t\) yields exactly a VE process at noise scale \(\tilde\sigma_t = \sigma_t/\alpha_t\) (the noise-to-signal ratio: with the usual \(\mathrm{SNR} = \alpha^2/\sigma^2\), this is \(\mathrm{SNR}^{-1/2}\)), and scores transform by the chain rule. VP is VE followed by a deterministic shrink.
One caution about a tempting shortcut. For static identities — the corruption formula, the posterior, the denoiser, Tweedie — setting \(\alpha_t = 1\) in a VP expression recovers the corresponding VE formula from W01–W02, and we use this check repeatedly below. For dynamics the shortcut fails: \(\alpha \equiv 1\) in VP forces \(\beta \equiv 0\), a frozen process. The dynamical bridge is the coordinate change above, not a parameter setting.

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
section: The forward SDE, and what it constructs
text:
The forward SDE, and what it constructs
A general diffusion process is specified by a stochastic differential equation
\[
\boxed{\ dX_t = f(X_t, t)\, dt + g(t)\, dW_t \ }
\]
with four ingredients: the state \(X_t \in \mathbb{R}^d\) (the sample at noise level \(t\), with \(X_0 \sim p_{\text{data}}\)); the time \(t \in [0, T]\), which is not physical time but a continuous corruption index; the drift \(f(x,t)\), the deterministic part of the motion (remove the noise term and the dynamics would be \(\dot X = f(X,t)\)); and the diffusion coefficient \(g(t)\) scaling the Brownian increments \(W_{t + dt} - W_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, dt\, I)\) — how much fresh noise is injected per unit of forward time.
The VP diffusion is the choice
\[
\boxed{\ dX_t = -\tfrac12 \beta(t)\, X_t\, dt + \sqrt{\beta(t)}\, dW_t \ }
\]
\[
f(x,t) = -\tfrac12\beta(t)\, x, \qquad g(t) = \sqrt{\beta(t)},
\]
where \(\beta(t) > 0\) is the noise schedule — the only coefficient choice within this VP family: it fixes the drift, the diffusion coefficient, and (below) the corruption parameters. Small \(\beta\) means slow corruption; the usual schedules increase \(\beta(t)\) so that early times perturb gently and late times destroy aggressively.
The name variance-preserving records a covariance identity. From the closed form below, \(\operatorname{Cov}(X_t) = \alpha_t^2 \operatorname{Cov}(X_0) +
(1 - \alpha_t^2) I\): any data law with unit covariance keeps covariance \(I\) for all \(t\) (and if \(X_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\), the entire law is stationary). For general data the intermediate laws are not Gaussian, but the variance scale stays controlled, and the law approaches \(\mathcal{N}(0, I)\) insofar as \(\alpha_t \to 0\).
The VP SDE admits a closed-form conditional description — for each fixed \(t\),
\[
\boxed{\ X_t \overset{d}{=} \alpha_t X_0 + \sigma_t \varepsilon, \qquad
\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) \text{ independent of } X_0 \ }
\]
\[
\alpha_t = \exp\!\Big(\!-\tfrac12 \int_0^t \beta(s)\, ds\Big),
\qquad \sigma_t^2 = 1 - \alpha_t^2 .
\]
(This is a distributional identity per time slice; a single fixed \(\varepsilon\) does not describe the joint law of the whole path — for that, the SDE itself is the object.) At \(t = 0\): \(\alpha_0 = 1\), \(\sigma_0 = 0\) — the data itself. As \(t\) grows, \(\alpha_t \to 0\) exactly when \(\int_0^t \beta \to \infty\); at any finite \(T\) with finite \(\int_0^T \beta\), \(\alpha_T\) is small but positive, and \(p_T \approx \mathcal{N}(0, I)\) is an approximation — a good one for standard schedules, and the first entry in the error inventory kept below.






The forward process is a construction, not a destruction



What the forward process constructs is more important than what it destroys: a continuous family of distributions
\[
p_0 = p_{\text{data}}
\;\longrightarrow\; p_t \;\longrightarrow\; p_T \approx \mathcal{N}(0, I),
\]
\[
p_t(x) = \int \mathcal{N}\big(x;\, \alpha_t x_0,\, \sigma_t^2 I\big)\,
p_0(dx_0)
\]
— the rescaled data law convolved with \(\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_t^2 I)\). Every later object of the theory — the score, the velocity field, the transport — is a property of this family, not of any single noisy sample.


(Writing \(p_0(dx_0)\) matters: the two-point example below has an atomic \(p_0\) with no density.) This family is the path along which the model will later transport probability mass; it is the VP version of the family \(\{p_\sigma\}\) whose 1-D portrait fills the W01–W02 demos. Note that the family depends jointly on the schedule and on \(p_{\text{data}}\): the schedule fixes the corruption kernel, the data fixes what gets corrupted.

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
text:
The score
For each intermediate distribution at \(t > 0\) (where \(p_t\) is a genuine smooth density, whatever \(p_0\) was), define the score:
\[
\boxed{\ s_t(x) = \nabla_x \log p_t(x). \ }
\]
Geometrically: read the density as a landscape; the score points uphill, toward locally more probable samples. It is local information only — a direction, not a destination. Two canonical computations:

Gaussian: for \(p = \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2 I)\), \(\nabla_x \log p(x) = -(x - \mu)/\sigma^2\), pointing at the mean; for \(\mathcal{N}(0, I)\), simply \(-x\).
The two-bump mixture of W01, whose score \(\big(\tanh(x/\sigma^2) - x\big)/\sigma^2\) you have already derived and watched drive the reverse flow.

Here is the crux of the learning problem. The conditional corruption law \(p_t(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}(\alpha_t x_0, \sigma_t^2 I)\) is fully known — the schedule fixed it. But the marginal \(p_t\) mixes the conditional over the unknown \(p_{\text{data}}\), so its score cannot be evaluated. The score is the only learned time-dependent function this sampler requires (the exact terminal law \(p_T\) also depends on the data, but it is approximated by a Gaussian rather than learned).

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
text:
Learning the score
Three objects must be kept distinct in this section; conflating any two of them is a standard error.
Object 1: the sampled conditional target. The forward process manufactures training data: draw \(x_0 \sim p_{\text{data}}\), a time \(t\) (from a range bounded away from \(0\), or with a weight that keeps the objective finite — see below), and \(\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\); form \(x_t = \alpha_t x_0 + \sigma_t
\varepsilon\). The conditional score is analytically available:
\[
\nabla_{x_t} \log p_t(x_t \mid x_0)
= -\frac{x_t - \alpha_t x_0}{\sigma_t^2}
= -\frac{\varepsilon}{\sigma_t}.
\]
This is a random target, different for every draw.
Object 2: the marginal score — the posterior mean of the target. Denoising score matching trains a network \(s_\theta(x, t)\) against Object 1:
\[
\boxed{\
\mathcal{L}(\theta)
= \mathbb{E}\left[ \lambda(t)\,
\Big\| s_\theta(x_t, t) + \frac{\varepsilon}{\sigma_t} \Big\|^2 \right],
\ }
\]
with \(\lambda(t) > 0\) a weighting choice. The reason this works: for each fixed \((x, t)\) with \(t > 0\), the minimizer of a conditional squared error is the conditional mean, and (differentiating under the integral)
\[
\begin{aligned}
s^\star(x, t)
&= \mathbb{E}\big[ \nabla_x \log p_t(x \mid x_0) \,\big|\, x_t = x \big]
= \frac{\int \nabla_x p_t(x \mid x_0)\, p_0(dx_0)}{p_t(x)} \\[2pt]
&= \frac{\nabla_x p_t(x)}{p_t(x)}
= \nabla_x \log p_t(x).
\end{aligned}
\]
The population minimizer over unrestricted functions is the marginal score; a neural network approximates it within its class. (Module 4 does this with full care — Vincent’s identity. Note also that with \(\lambda \equiv 1\) the target variance behaves like \(1/\sigma_t^2\) near \(t = 0\), which is why practical recipes either weight or avoid the smallest times.)
Object 3: the noise-predictor parameterization. Many implementations train \(\varepsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\) to predict the injected noise. Its population optimum is the posterior mean \(\varepsilon^\star(x, t) = \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon
\mid x_t = x]\) — not the per-sample \(\varepsilon\) — and the two optima are linked by
\[
s^\star(x, t) = -\frac{\varepsilon^\star(x, t)}{\sigma_t},
\qquad\text{hence one trains with}\qquad
s_\theta = -\frac{\varepsilon_\theta}{\sigma_t}.
\]
Score prediction and noise prediction are the same estimator in different units; a score loss with weight \(\lambda(t)\) equals a noise loss with weight \(\lambda(t)/\sigma_t^2\).






“Noise prediction” is conditional-mean estimation



The account above is the standard one and its algebra is correct — but the phrase “the network predicts the injected noise”, read literally, is misleading, and it quietly breeds specific misconceptions (collected at the end of this box, each traced to its root). Nor is the phrase a strawman: it is the research literature’s own language, verbatim. The DDPM paper introduces the network as “a function approximator intended to predict \(\varepsilon\) from \(\mathbf{x}_t\)”1; the DDIM paper writes that “the model \(\varepsilon_\theta^{(t)}(\mathbf{x}_t)\) then attempts to predict \(\varepsilon_t\) from \(\mathbf{x}_t\), without knowledge of \(\mathbf{x}_0\)”2; Nichol and Dhariwal state that “the network could also predict the noise \(\varepsilon\)” and that “predicting \(\varepsilon\) worked best”3. The expository canon carries it further: the widely used Hugging Face implementation guide describes the reparametrization as making “the neural network learn (predict) the added noise” and concludes that “our neural network becomes a noise predictor, rather than a (direct) mean predictor”4 — a phrasing worth savoring, since the population-optimal noise predictor is a mean predictor, of the conditional kind. Careful statements do exist in print — the tutorial of Nakkiran et al. presents \(\varepsilon\)-, \(x_0\)-, and \(v\)-prediction uniformly as estimation of conditional expectations5 — but they are the exception, not the phrasing that spread. The phrasing is harmless to authors who hold the algebra in their heads — and misleading to every reader who does not. (One terminological note: throughout, \(\varepsilon\) denotes the aggregate noise of the fixed-\(t\) representation \(x_t = \alpha_t x_0 + \sigma_t \varepsilon\) — the object the literature’s phrase refers to — not the one-step innovation between adjacent times.)
\[
\varepsilon
= \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid x_t, t]}_{\displaystyle \varepsilon^\star(x_t, t)}
+ \underbrace{\big(\varepsilon - \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid x_t, t]\big)}_{\text{zero conditional mean}} ,
\]
the first term a deterministic function of what the network sees, the second a residual with zero conditional mean (not independent of the observation — only its best point prediction is exhausted). For any predictor that is a function of \((x_t, t)\), the tower property splits the loss accordingly:
\[
\mathbb{E}\big\|\varepsilon_\theta - \varepsilon\big\|^2
= \mathbb{E}\big\|\varepsilon_\theta - \varepsilon^\star\big\|^2
+ \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\big\|\varepsilon - \varepsilon^\star\big\|^2}_{\text{irreducible floor}}
\]
(a time-dependent weight \(\lambda(t)\) multiplies both terms alike). Only the first term is reducible in population risk. The floor equals \(\mathbb{E}\, \operatorname{tr} \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon \mid x_t, t)\) — the minimum mean-squared error — and for nondegenerate data at finite noise levels it is strictly positive: the training loss does not approach zero, and should not.
The reducible part is an object we have already met:
\[
\varepsilon^\star(x, t) = -\sigma_t\, s_t(x)
\]
— the negative, \(\sigma_t\)-scaled score. The predictable component of the noise encodes exactly the score, and nothing more. Equivalently, in displacement form: \(\sigma_t\, \varepsilon^\star(x,t) = x - \alpha_t\, \mathbb{E}[X_0 \mid x]
= -\sigma_t^2 s_t(x)\) — the posterior-mean offset of the observation from the attenuated clean signal (a mean, not a most-likely value). It is a deterministic, smoothly varying field: for the two-point example below, \(\varepsilon^\star(x,t) = \big(x - \alpha_t \tanh(\alpha_t x/\sigma_t^2)\big)/\sigma_t\), a smooth curve in \(x\).
The confusion has a simple source. In a regression there are two different objects: the target — the random quantity each training pair happens to contain (here, the sampled \(\varepsilon\)) — and the fitted function — what the trained model actually computes, namely the average of all targets compatible with a given input (here, \(\varepsilon^\star\)). The phrase “noise prediction” names the target; the network is the fitted function. In careful regression language the phrase is even defensible — predicting a random target means estimating its conditional mean — but the colloquial reading of “noise” hides that this is what is happening.
Two consequences sharpen the picture.

Structure in the data appears as the nonlinear part of the conditional-mean field — and that field, not any randomness, is what the network learns. For data with no data-specific structure (\(p_{\text{data}} = \mathcal{N}(0, I)\), so \(p_t = \mathcal{N}(0, I)\) and \(s_t(x) = -x\)), the field reduces to the linear baseline \(\varepsilon^\star = \sigma_t x\); in the probability-flow ODE this score exactly cancels the VP drift — zero velocity, nothing to transport.
How much of the noise is predictable depends on the data and the noise level. For smooth, full-dimensional data, \(\mathbb{E}\|\varepsilon^\star\|^2 = \sigma_t^2\, J(p_t) \to 0\) as \(\sigma_t \to 0\) (with \(J\) the Fisher information): the standardized noise becomes mostly unpredictable even though denoising is easy. For atomic or well-separated data — the two-point example — the nearby atom becomes identifiable at small \(\sigma_t\) and the noise becomes nearly recoverable from the observation. At the other extreme (\(\sigma_t \to 1\), \(\alpha_t \to 0\)), \(x_t \to \varepsilon\) and prediction is trivial: the observation mostly is the noise.

The root cause, and the three misconceptions it breeds. Each falsehood below is a logical consequence of taking “the network predicts the noise” literally; each is followed by the correcting fact.

If the noise can truly be predicted, the training loss should reach zero. — In fact the loss is bounded below by \(\mathbb{E}\, \operatorname{tr} \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon \mid x_t, t) > 0\) for nondegenerate data at finite noise level; no function of \((x_t, t)\) can go beneath it.
If what is being predicted is “noise”, the prediction should look like static and jitter. — In fact the fitted function is a deterministic field: evaluated twice at the same \((x_t, t)\) it returns the same answer, and it varies smoothly with its input — the two-point formula above is a \(\tanh\) curve, not a jitter. (Its values can occasionally resemble a noise pattern — for Gaussian data \(\varepsilon^\star = \sigma_t x_t\) — but it is a fixed function of the input, never a fresh random draw.)
If the network predicts noise, it has the strange ability to predict randomness. — In fact it estimates a conditional mean: the structured component \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid x_t, t]\), the part of the noise that the observation determines. The genuinely random residual is never predicted by anything.

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
section: From SDE to ODE: the derivation
text:
From SDE to ODE: the derivation
This is the heart of the tutorial. The density of the forward SDE evolves by the Fokker–Planck equation (Module 5 derives it; here we use it):
\[
\boxed{\
\frac{\partial p_t}{\partial t}
= -\nabla \cdot (f\, p_t) + \tfrac12 g(t)^2\, \Delta p_t
\ }
\]
— deterministic transport by the drift, plus spreading by the noise. Separately, purely deterministic particle motion \(\dot X_t = v(X_t, t)\) evolves its density by the continuity equation:
\[
\frac{\partial p_t}{\partial t} = -\nabla \cdot (p_t\, v).
\]
The question writes itself: is there a velocity field \(v\) whose noiseless transport reproduces exactly the density evolution of the noisy SDE? Try
\[
v(x, t) = f(x, t) - \tfrac12 g(t)^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(x).
\]
Then, using \(p_t \nabla \log p_t = \nabla p_t\),
\[
p_t v = p_t f - \tfrac12 g^2\, p_t \nabla \log p_t
      = p_t f - \tfrac12 g^2\, \nabla p_t,
\]
so
\[
-\nabla \cdot (p_t v)
= -\nabla \cdot (p_t f) + \tfrac12 g^2\, \nabla \cdot (\nabla p_t)
= -\nabla \cdot (p_t f) + \tfrac12 g^2\, \Delta p_t
\]
— exactly the Fokker–Planck right-hand side. The diffusion term has been absorbed into an extra drift along the score (in forward time the correction points down the score, spreading mass; integrated backward it points up). Hence the deterministic dynamics
\[
\boxed{\
\frac{dX_t}{dt} = f(X_t, t) - \tfrac12 g(t)^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(X_t)
\ }
\]
reproduces the marginals \(p_t\) on any interval \([\epsilon, T]\) with \(\epsilon > 0\), when initialized from the matching law at either end (from \(p_T\), integrated backward, for generation). If \(p_0\) itself is singular — the two-point example — the flow reaches it only in the \(\epsilon \downarrow 0\) limit: a smooth flow cannot terminate on atoms at any positive time, which is the VP face of the \(\sigma_{\min}\) discussion in the earlier tutorials. This is the probability-flow ODE. For VP diffusion it takes a compact form:
\[
\boxed{\
\frac{dX_t}{dt} = -\tfrac12 \beta(t)\, \big[ X_t + s_t(X_t) \big],
\ }
\]
and with the learned score, \(s_t \to s_\theta\). (In \(d > 1\) this velocity is the canonical choice, not the unique one: adding any field \(u\) with \(\nabla\!\cdot(p_t u) = 0\) preserves the same marginals. In one dimension the monotone flow is unique — the rigidity used below.)
One box on the stochastic alternative, for completeness. Introduce the increasing reverse clock \(\tau = T - t\), so that “later” means “less noisy”; then the same score defines the reverse-time SDE
\[
dX = \big[ -f(X, t) + g(t)^2\, s_t(X) \big]\, d\tau + g(t)\, d\bar W_\tau ,
\]
with \(\bar W\) a fresh Brownian motion in the \(\tau\) clock. Note the score coefficient \(g^2\) — twice the ODE’s \(\tfrac12 g^2\) — compensating the re-injected noise: the same doubling you saw in the two-point sampler of W01. With the exact score and exact initialization from \(p_T\), both samplers traverse the same family \(\{p_t\}\); the ODE is deterministic given \(X_T\), the SDE consumes fresh randomness at every instant. From here on we follow the ODE.
Two readings of the result:

Kinematic: the equation is first-order — it prescribes velocity, not force. Every point of space-time carries an arrow \(v(x,t)\); a particle follows the arrow under its feet, and the arrows change both because the particle moves and because the field is time-dependent.
Hydrodynamic: release many particles from \(p_T\) and let each follow the field; individually deterministic, collectively their density flows — the continuity equation is conservation of probability mass. Hence the name: probability flows through space under a deterministic velocity field.

And the answer to a question worth asking out loud: is the score the velocity? No. The velocity is drift plus score correction,
\[
v = \underbrace{f}_{\text{known from the schedule}}
- \underbrace{\tfrac12 g^2\, s}_{\text{learned correction}},
\]
with the schedule deciding how strongly the learned geometry steers the motion.

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
text:
Sampling is numerical integration
After training, everything on the right-hand side of the ODE is available: the schedule supplies \(\beta(t)\) — hence \(f\), \(g\), \(\alpha_t\), \(\sigma_t\) — and the network supplies \(s_\theta(x, t)\). Generation is: draw \(X_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\) (the Gaussian stand-in for \(p_T\)), integrate backward to \(t = \epsilon\), return the endpoint. But the trajectory is defined implicitly — \(v\) depends on the state along the unknown path — so for a neural score there is generally no closed form. The trajectory is computed numerically.
Fix a descending grid \(T = t_N > t_{N-1} > \cdots > t_1 > t_0 = \epsilon\), with \(h_k = t_{k-1} - t_k < 0\) (backward steps), and \(\epsilon > 0\) a small final time. The Euler sampler:
\[
\boxed{\
\begin{aligned}
&X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) \\
&\text{for } k = N, N-1, \dots, 1: \\
&\qquad s \leftarrow s_\theta(X, t_k) \\
&\qquad v \leftarrow -\tfrac12 \beta(t_k)\, (X + s) \\
&\qquad X \leftarrow X + h_k\, v \\
&\text{return } X
\end{aligned}
\ }
\]
Since \(h_k < 0\), the score increment is \(+\tfrac12 \beta(t_k)\, |h_k|\,
s_\theta\) — the particle steps up the score, consistent with W01’s sampler. Four remarks that carry more weight than the pseudocode:

The score must be re-evaluated at every step. Both of its arguments change: the particle moved, and the noise level dropped. Each step is evaluate score → construct velocity → move → repeat — the sampler incrementally reconstructs a global transport from local information.
Better integrators exist. Heun’s method: take the provisional Euler step \(X^* = X_k + h_k\, v(X_k, t_k)\), re-evaluate the velocity at the provisional state and the new time, \(v^* = v(X^*, t_{k-1})\), then move by the average, \(X_{k-1} = X_k + \tfrac{h_k}{2}\big( v(X_k, t_k) + v^* \big)\) — second-order accuracy (for sufficiently smooth fields) at two network calls per step. Beyond it: Runge–Kutta, adaptive solvers, multistep and diffusion-specific schemes. The relevant cost metric is the number of neural function evaluations (NFE), since each velocity evaluation runs the network once.
The four errors, inventoried (mirroring the W01 tutorial’s honesty paragraph): (i) terminal-prior mismatch — sampling \(\mathcal{N}(0, I)\) instead of the true \(p_T\); (ii) score error — \(s_\theta \ne s_t\); (iii) integration error — finite steps; (iv) finite-\(\epsilon\) endpoint bias — stopping at \(t = \epsilon\). Under exact prior, exact score, and exact integration, the endpoint law is exactly \(p_\epsilon\); the practical sampler carries all four deviations.
The \(\epsilon\)-endpoint is not a technicality. Even the idealized endpoint \(p_\epsilon\) is the attenuated and smoothed data law (\(\alpha_\epsilon X_0 + \sigma_\epsilon Z\)), not the data law itself — the VP twin of the terminal width \(\sigma_{\min}\) quantified in the W01 tutorial and The Deterministic Map, Proved. Increasing the step count removes integration error only; lowering \(\epsilon\) sharpens the target, at the price of an increasingly stiff velocity field (for the two-point score below, the derivative at the separatrix scales like \(\sigma_t^{-4}\)).

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
section: The two-point example, in VP coordinates
text:
The two-point example, in VP coordinates
Now run the entire pipeline on the course’s home dataset, \(p_0 = \tfrac12 \delta_{-1} + \tfrac12 \delta_{+1}\) — the case where every learned object has a formula, worked in the VE convention in the W01 tutorial and proved in The Deterministic Map, Proved. Conditioning on the component, \(X_t \mid X_0 = \pm 1 \sim \mathcal{N}(\pm\alpha_t, \sigma_t^2)\), so
\[
p_t(x) = \tfrac12\, \mathcal{N}(x; -\alpha_t, \sigma_t^2)
       + \tfrac12\, \mathcal{N}(x; +\alpha_t, \sigma_t^2)
\]
(sanity check: \(\operatorname{Var}(X_t) = \alpha_t^2 + \sigma_t^2 = 1\) — variance preserved exactly). The posterior is one line of Bayes — the likelihood ratio of the two components is \(\exp(-2\alpha_t x/\sigma_t^2)\), so
\[
\mathbb{P}(X_0 = +1 \mid X_t = x)
= \operatorname{sigmoid}\!\Big( \frac{2 \alpha_t x}{\sigma_t^2} \Big),
\]
\[
\widehat X_0(x, t) := \mathbb{E}[X_0 \mid X_t = x]
= \tanh\!\Big( \frac{\alpha_t x}{\sigma_t^2} \Big),
\]
and the score follows in one more line from VP Tweedie (\(s = (\alpha_t\, \mathbb{E}[X_0 \mid x] - x)/\sigma_t^2\), derived in the next section):
\[
s_t(x) = \frac{ \alpha_t \tanh(\alpha_t x / \sigma_t^2) - x }{ \sigma_t^2 },
\]
\[
v_t(x) = -\tfrac12 \beta(t)
\left[ x + \frac{ \alpha_t \tanh(\alpha_t x/\sigma_t^2) - x }{ \sigma_t^2 } \right].
\]
Setting \(\alpha_t = 1\) recovers every corresponding W01 formula — the static dictionary at work. As \(t \to 0\): \(\alpha_t \to 1\), \(\sigma_t \to 0\), so \(\widehat X_0(x, t) \to \operatorname{sign}(x)\) pointwise for \(x \ne 0\) (not uniformly near \(0\)) — the smooth \(\tanh\) denoiser sharpening into the discontinuous sign map.
What does the integrated flow do? The 1-D argument of The Deterministic Map, Proved runs in two stages, and the order matters. Stage one, at positive noise: for each \(\epsilon > 0\), the flow map \(\Psi_{T \to \epsilon}\) is continuous and strictly increasing (trajectories of a smooth 1-D ODE cannot cross), and a monotone map pushing \(p_T\) to \(p_\epsilon\) is unique — therefore
\[
\Psi_{T \to \epsilon} = F_\epsilon^{-1} \circ F_T ,
\]
the quantile transport between the two mixture CDFs. (At finite \(T\), \(F_T\) is the CDF of the near-Gaussian mixture, not of \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\); by symmetry both place their median at \(0\), which is all the limit needs.) Stage two, the limit: as \(\epsilon \downarrow 0\), the target collapses onto the atoms and
\[
\boxed{\ \Psi_{T \to \epsilon}(X_T) \;\longrightarrow\; \operatorname{sign}(X_T)
\qquad p_T\text{-almost surely}. \ }
\]
Every positive start ends at \(+1\), every negative start at \(-1\), and symmetry sends exactly half the mass to each atom. For the smoothed target \(\tfrac12\mathcal{N}(-1, \varrho^2) + \tfrac12\mathcal{N}(+1, \varrho^2)\) the finite-\(T\) endpoint map is the genuine quantile transport \(F_{0,\varrho}^{-1} \circ F_T\) (which becomes \(F_{0,\varrho}^{-1} \circ \Phi\) only in the idealized exactly-Gaussian-terminal limit), converging to the sign map as \(\varrho \to 0\).
One qualification keeps the example honest. In this special symmetric case the endpoint of the flow happens to be a formula we could have written down without any ODE. The solver is not “numerically approximating the sign function” in general: it solves a differential equation whose endpoint, for arbitrary data, is not known in advance — that is the entire point of learning the score.

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
section: Three distinctions that prevent three confusions
text:
Three distinctions that prevent three confusions
The score is not the velocity. \(v = f - \tfrac12 g^2 s\): the learned score is the correction; the schedule contributes the drift and decides the correction’s strength.
The denoiser is not the endpoint. VP Tweedie (set \(\alpha \equiv 1\) to recover W01’s version) gives the one-step posterior mean
\[
\mathbb{E}[X_0 \mid X_t = x] = \frac{x + \sigma_t^2\, s_t(x)}{\alpha_t}
\qquad (\alpha_t > 0),
\]
a single denoising estimate from noise level \(t\). The flow endpoint \(\Psi_{T \to \epsilon}(X_T)\) integrates the score field through every level. In the two-point limit both converge to the same sign decision — because a trajectory that never touches \(0\) keeps its sign, and the denoiser’s sign at any level agrees with it — but they are different objects, and conflating them is a common reading error in the literature.
The one-shot map and the incremental flow solve the same problem. Define the per-step Euler map \(E_k(x) = x + h_k\, v(x, t_k)\). Then the endpoint transport is represented implicitly as a time-ordered composition,
\[
\Psi_{T \to \epsilon}
= \lim_{\max_k |h_k| \to 0}\; E_1 \circ E_2 \circ \cdots \circ E_N ,
\]
— the factorization view of The Deterministic Map, Proved, now with a learned field: each factor is near-identity and needs only local information. For fixed \(\epsilon > 0\) this limit is a continuous map; any discontinuity (the sign function) arises only in the separate limit \(\epsilon \downarrow 0\).

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
The Probability-Flow ODE
text:
Takeaways

The schedule \(\beta(t)\) determines the corruption kernel — drift, diffusion coefficient, \(\alpha_t\), \(\sigma_t\); together with the data it determines the family \(\{p_t\}\).
The score \(\nabla \log p_t\) is the only learned time-dependent function the sampler needs, trained by denoising score matching on synthetically corrupted data; noise prediction is the same estimator in different units, with population optimum \(-\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid x_t]/\sigma_t\).
The probability-flow ODE replaces the SDE’s noise by an extra drift along the score, reproducing the same marginals deterministically on \([\epsilon, T]\): \(v = f - \tfrac12 g^2 s\).
Sampling is numerical ODE integration; each step is score evaluation → velocity → move; accuracy is bought with NFE; and the practical sampler carries four distinct errors — prior mismatch, score error, integration error, and the finite-\(\epsilon\) endpoint bias.
In the two-point limit the integrated flow converges to the sign map — locally learned gradients, integrated into a transport that is discontinuous only in the \(\epsilon \downarrow 0\) limit — and for real data the same principle holds with no formula available: the global generative transformation is obtained by integrating locally learned score information.

title: The Probability-Flow ODE
text:
Exercises

(One-dimensional.) Verify from the closed form \(X_t \overset{d}{=} \alpha_t X_0 + \sigma_t \varepsilon\) that \(\operatorname{Var}(X_t) = \alpha_t^2 \operatorname{Var}(X_0) + \sigma_t^2\), and confirm the variance-preserving property for unit-variance data. State the \(d\)-dimensional covariance version.
Use the static dictionary (\(\alpha \equiv 1\)) to recover, from the VP two-point formulas: the mixture \(p_t\), the posterior, the denoiser, and the score — and match each against the W01 tutorial. Then use the dynamic dictionary (\(Y = X/\alpha\)) to transform the VP score into the VE score and check consistency.
Complete the proof that the population minimizer of the denoising score-matching objective is the marginal score, stating explicitly where \(t > 0\), \(\lambda(t) > 0\), and differentiation under the integral are used.
Show that the reverse-time SDE and the probability-flow ODE differ exactly by replacing \(\tfrac12 g^2 s\, dt\) with \(g^2 s\, dt - g\, d\bar W\), and argue via the Fokker–Planck equation that both preserve the family \(\{p_t\}\) under exact score and exact terminal initialization.
A reproducible benchmark. Take \(\beta(t) = 0.1 + 19.9\,t\) on \([0, 1]\) (so \(\alpha_t = e^{-(0.05 t + 4.975 t^2)}\)), \(\epsilon = 10^{-3}\), a uniform grid in \(t\), exact two-point score, and \(X_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\). Measure the RMS distance of endpoints to the nearest atom. Compare Euler and Heun at equal NFE (Euler gets twice the steps). Which wins at NFE = 10? At NFE = 100?
For the smoothed two-point target with component variance \(\varrho^2\), write the VP forward family \(p_t\) explicitly (hint: Gaussians convolve), and verify that the finite-\(T\) quantile transport is \(F_{0,\varrho}^{-1} \circ F_T\), reducing to \(F_{0,\varrho}^{-1} \circ \Phi\) only when \(p_T\) is replaced by its Gaussian idealization.
For the two-point score, compute \(s_t'(0)\) and show it scales as \(\alpha_t^2/\sigma_t^4\) for small \(\sigma_t\) — the stiffness quoted in the sampling section. Where in \(x\) is \(|s_t'|\) largest, and why is that exactly where a numerical integrator needs small steps?

title: Generative Models as Transport: History and Validation
text:
The thesis, and two category errors to avoid
The folklore version of the transport view says: generative modeling is fundamentally transport; in 1-D the inverse CDF solves it completely and all model families coincide there; in higher dimension the transport is no longer unique, and VAEs, GANs, flows, and diffusion models are different general constructions. This is close to right — and wrong in two instructive ways.
Category error 1: representation is not explanation. On standard Borel spaces, essentially every distribution is the pushforward of a uniform random variable by some measurable map; a stochastic sampler becomes a deterministic one after adjoining its auxiliary noise to the source. “Every generative model is a transport” is therefore nearly tautological — a representation available for anything, not a characterization of anything. What the transport language genuinely does not capture: tractability of the likelihood (flows buy it with Jacobians, the probability-flow ODE with divergence integration, VAEs with an evidence bound, GANs not at all); conditioning (a coherent family \(p(dx \mid c)\) is more structure than an endpoint map); stochastic kernels (a VAE decoder is a Markov kernel, not a map, and its encoder approximates a posterior kernel, not an inverse); and — decisively for what follows — coupling identification: two maps can have identical pushforwards and completely different input–output correspondences. Matching the endpoint law does not identify the map.
Category error 2: 1-D uniqueness is a property of a selection rule, not of dimension. Even on the real line, transport is wildly nonunique: both \(u \mapsto u\) and \(u \mapsto 1-u\) carry \(\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)\) to itself, and composing any generator with a source-preserving map changes nothing about the output law. What dimension one possesses is a uniquely privileged selection: the total order, and with it the requirement “order-preserving,” which singles out one map. Higher dimensions do not lose transport; they lose the privileged tie-breaker.
With both corrections made, the thesis survives in a sharper form, stated at the end of this tutorial. The body earns it.

Dimension one: the complete theory of order-compatible transport
Fix probability measures \(\mu,

Fact 1 (generation always works — atoms included). \(Q_{

\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1) =

u\) on \(\mathbb{R}\). The quantile coupling \(\gamma^\uparrow = (Q_\mu, Q_
u)_\#\, \mathrm{Leb}_{(0,1)}\) exists for arbitrary \(\mu, 
u\) and is the canonical order-preserving (comonotone) coupling. (Standard; see Santambrogio, Optimal Transport for Applied Mathematicians, Ch. 2.)
Fact 2 (uniqueness, under the order selection, for atomless sources). If \(\mu\) is atomless, then \(T = Q_
u \circ F_\mu\) is the unique nondecreasing map with \(T_\# \mu = 
u\), up to \(\mu\)-null sets. The target may be atomic — this course’s two-point distribution is generated by exactly such a map, and the full proof is in The Deterministic Map, Proved (Theorem 1 and Propositions 2 and 7 there).
Fact 3 (optimality, for free). The same monotone map is optimal for every convex displacement cost \(c(x - y)\) — a universality that is essentially one-dimensional and will fail upstairs.
Fact 4 (the honest direction of the atomic caveat). The failure mode is not generation into atomic targets — that always works — but deterministic encoding out of atomic sources: a source atom cannot be split by a map, so no deterministic encoder carries atomic data onto a continuous prior. The canonical repair is stochastic — Rüschendorf’s distributional transform \(U = F_\mu(X^-) + V\,(F_\mu(X) - F_\mu(X^-))\) with \(V \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)\) independent, which is exactly uniform even when \(X\) has atoms. (Randomized rank-breaking of ties: the coin flip of the informal tutorial.)
So the precise sense in which dimension one is “completely understood”: order-compatible transport on the line has an explicit, generalized-quantile solution in all cases. Not solved by this: transport under other selections, statistical estimation, or learnability — distinctions that matter below.

section: Dimension two and above: underdeterminacy, and the selection principles
text:
Dimension two and above: underdeterminacy, and the selection principles
Endpoint marginals never determine a coupling: if \(T_\# \rho = \mu\) and \(S_\# \rho = \rho\), then \((T \circ S)_\# \rho = \mu\). In \(d \ge 2\) the supply of source-preserving maps \(S\) is enormous, and — the genuine loss — no total order exists to privilege one choice. There is a second, subtler underdeterminacy at the level of dynamics: for the continuity equation \(\partial_t p + \nabla\!\cdot(p v) = 0\), if \(v\) transports the path \(\{p_t\}\) then so does \(v + w\) for any \(w\) with \(\nabla\!\cdot(p w) = 0\) — weighted divergence-free “gauge” fields, abundant in \(d \ge 2\), invisible in \(d = 1\) (no room to swirl on a line). Even a prescribed marginal path does not determine particle trajectories; a current must be chosen too.
Each classical and each modern construction is a selection principle — something added to the marginal-matching requirement to pin down a map, a coupling, or a path. The audit table (each row’s qualification is part of the claim):








Construction
What selects
Essential qualification




Brenier / optimal transport
minimize squared displacement
unique map \(T = \nabla \phi\), \(\phi\) convex, for absolutely continuous sources with second moments — canonical relative to Euclidean quadratic geometry (Brenier 1991; McCann 1995)


Knothe–Rosenblatt
sequential conditional quantiles
unique monotone triangular map after fixing a coordinate order; not rotation-invariant, generally not optimal (Rosenblatt 1952; Knothe 1957; Carlier–Galichon–Santambrogio 2009)


Autoregressive flows
triangular architecture + likelihood
an expressive monotone triangular flow can recover KR; permuted stacks need not equal any single KR map (Irons et al. 2022)


General normalizing flows
architecture, orientation, optimization
maximum likelihood identifies the density, not the map


Diffusion / probability-flow ODE
forward SDE + schedule + score + choice of current
the path \(\{p_t\}\) alone does not fix the velocity in \(d \ge 2\); the gradient-form (curl-free relative to \(p\)) current is part of the selection


Flow matching / rectified flow
endpoint coupling + interpolant + regression
different couplings/interpolants give different fields with identical endpoints (Lipman et al. 2023; Liu et al. 2023)


GAN
none
any transport fooling the discriminator is accepted; even WGAN’s optimal-transport problem lives between the real and generated laws in data space — it does not select a latent-to-data map (Goodfellow et al. 2014; Arjovsky et al. 2017)


VAE
ELBO + prior + decoder noise + architecture
selects a generally nonidentifiable joint model and posterior kernel, not a Monge map


Schrödinger bridge
path-space relative entropy to a reference process
the principled stochastic transport selection (Léonard 2014)



And the statistics community, needing multivariate quantiles for its own reasons, ran the same route: the center-outward distribution functions of Chernozhukov–Galichon–Hallin–Henry (2017) and Hallin et al. (2021, arXiv:1806.01238) define the multivariate CDF as the Brenier map to a reference spherical law — canonical relative to that chosen reference geometry, not choice-free. The lesson of the whole table in one line: beyond dimension one, “the transport” is a category mistake; only “the transport selected by ⟨rule⟩” is well-posed.

title: Generative Models as Transport: History and Validation
section: The 1-D coincidences, stratified by epistemic status
text:
The 1-D coincidences, stratified by epistemic status
The folklore says “all families coincide with the quantile map in 1-D.” The truth splits three ways, and the split is the pedagogy.
Theorem-level (all exact scalar ODE samplers — one proof covers them). Let \(\{p_t\}\) be a smooth positive scalar density path with velocity \(v\) solving the continuity equation with zero flux at \(-\infty\). Then \(\partial_t F_t = -p_t v_t\), and along any characteristic \(\dot X = v_t(X)\): \(\frac{d}{dt} F_t(X_t) = 0\) — quantile labels are conserved, so the endpoint map is the quantile transport. This single argument covers the diffusion probability-flow ODE (proved in full, with numerics, in The Deterministic Map, Proved), continuous normalizing flows, flow matching, and rectified flow at the exact/population level; the distinctions among them are about how \(p_t\) and \(v_t\) are chosen and estimated, not about the exact 1-D endpoint. Monotone discrete-time flows join by Fact 2 directly. (Practical training adds estimation and integration error — conditionality of practice, not of mathematics.)
Available-but-not-selected (GANs). An explicit counterexample: with \(U \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)\), the tent map \(s(u) = 2u \wedge (2 - 2u)\) preserves uniformity, so \(Q_\mu(s(U))\) generates \(\mu\) exactly — and is not the quantile map. No idealized adversarial objective can distinguish it from \(Q_\mu(U)\): marginal matching leaves the generator unidentified. The coincidence is available to a GAN and never implied by its training.
Available-only-in-a-singular-idealization (VAEs). The precise proposition: if data and latent are scalar and atomless, the prior has continuous strictly increasing CDF \(H\), the encoder \(E\) and decoder \(D\) are deterministic, mutually inverse a.e., aggregate-matched ($E_# = $ prior), nondecreasing, and exactly optimized, then Fact 2 forces \(E = H^{-1} \circ F_\mu\) and \(D = Q_\mu \circ H\) — with a uniform prior, literally \(E = F_\mu\), \(D = Q_\mu\). Every hypothesis earns its place: drop monotonicity and the decreasing solution (and worse) appears; and a strict VAE cannot even enter this idealization — a deterministic encoder against a continuous prior has infinite KL penalty (\(\mathrm{KL}(\mathcal{N}(E(x), \sigma^2) \,\|\, \mathcal{N}(0,1)) \to \infty\) as \(\sigma \downarrow 0\)), and an expressive decoder admits posterior collapse (\(p_\theta(x \mid z) = p_{\text{data}}\), encoder carrying no information) which fits the marginal perfectly with no CDF anywhere. Identifiability theory does not rescue the slogan: the identifiable-VAE results of Khemakhem et al. (2020) require auxiliary observed variables and structured priors, deliver identification only up to linear/permutation ambiguities, and do not apply to the ordinary unconditional VAE — consistent with the classical nonidentifiability of nonlinear ICA (Hyvärinen–Pajunen 1999) and the impossibility results for unsupervised disentanglement (Locatello et al. 2019). The idealized object is better named a monotone scalar normalizing flow (or a Wasserstein-autoencoder-style construction, whose objective — Tolstikhin et al. 2018 — does regularize the aggregate encoding, unlike the VAE’s). The slogan “the encoder is the CDF” is a theorem about that idealized object and a false statement about VAE training.
The three-way split generalizes into the distinction this tutorial exists to teach:

For any generative method, ask three separate questions. (1) Existence: can it represent a transport achieving the target law? (2) Selection: does its construction single out which transport? (3) Identification: does its training objective actually enforce that selection? In 1-D, exact scalar ODE methods answer yes–yes–yes (order is built into non-crossing); GANs answer yes–no–no; VAEs answer yes–no–no with an extra obstruction (kernels, not maps). The families feel identical in 1-D only if one asks question (1) alone.

title: Generative Models as Transport: History and Validation
section: What breaks upstairs: the misleading-intuitions inventory
text:
What breaks upstairs: the misleading-intuitions inventory
Each entry is a 1-D truth that fails in \(d \ge 2\) — with the failure’s certificate.

“Transport is unique.” Never was — uniqueness belonged to the order selection, which does not exist upstairs.
“Non-crossing implies the canonical map.” In \(d \ge 2\) trajectories can rotate and swirl without intersecting; orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms need not be (cyclically) monotone or optimal.
“A gradient velocity field integrates to a gradient map.” False: time-ordered products of symmetric Jacobians lose symmetry when Hessians at different times fail to commute. This is precisely the mechanism of Lavenant–Santambrogio (2022) (Appl. Math. Lett.): a smooth two-dimensional example where the Fokker–Planck flow map is a perfectly valid transport to the Gaussian and not the Brenier map — written to refute a published conjecture (Khrulkov–Oseledets 2022) that assumed otherwise. The 1-D coincidence misled professionals in print.
“The marginal path determines the particle paths.” Only on the line, where zero-flux kills the ambiguity. Upstairs, divergence-free currents are a genuine gauge freedom; the diffusion velocity is a choice of current.
“Componentwise CDFs are a multivariate rank.” They uniformize marginals and leave the entire dependence structure (the copula) untouched; Rosenblatt’s transform fixes this at the price of coordinate-order dependence.
“Monotone becomes meaningless.” It becomes plural: coordinatewise isotonicity, monotone operators, triangular monotonicity, and cyclic monotonicity are inequivalent notions — and different selection principles commit to different ones (Brenier: cyclic; KR: triangular).
“One map is optimal for all convex costs.” Essentially one-dimensional. Upstairs the selected map depends on the cost and the geometry.
“Low-dimensional pictures scale.” \(\|Z\| \approx \sqrt{d}\) for \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)\) — mass lives on shells, not at the mode; and empirical transport estimation suffers dimension-dependent rates of order \(n^{-1/d}\) (Weed–Bach 2019). The 1-D laboratory is a laboratory, not a scale model.

text:
A short history, as the pedagogy’s spine







Year
Event




1781
Monge poses the transport problem (déblais et remblais)


1942
Kantorovich relaxes maps to couplings — transport becomes tractable


1952 / 1957
Rosenblatt’s transformation; Knothe’s rearrangement — the coordinate-order selection


1991 / 1995
Brenier’s polar factorization; McCann’s refinements — the cost selection, uniqueness restored in \(d \ge 2\)


2013–2014
VAEs (Kingma–Welling); GANs (Goodfellow et al.) — learned transports with variational and adversarial objectives, no map selection


2015–2017
Normalizing flows mature (Rezende–Mohamed; autoregressive = triangular ≈ KR); WGAN imports the OT metric (not the OT map)


2015–2021
Diffusion: nonequilibrium thermodynamics (Sohl-Dickstein et al.), DDPM (Ho et al.), score SDE and probability-flow ODE (Song et al.) — the dynamic selection


2017–2021
Statistics rebuilds the CDF via transport: Monge–Kantorovich depth, center-outward distribution functions (Chernozhukov et al.; Hallin et al.)


2022
Khrulkov–Oseledets conjecture the diffusion flow is OT; Lavenant–Santambrogio refute it — the 1-D coincidence formally dies in \(d \ge 2\)


2022–2023
Flow matching (Lipman et al.), rectified flow (Liu et al.), stochastic interpolants (Albergo–Boffi–Vanden-Eijnden) — the coupling-and-interpolant selection made explicit



The pedagogy of this course tracks that history in miniature: quantiles first, then the loss of order, then the selections — and the stochastic-interpolant viewpoint, in which coupling, interpolant, velocity, and noise are all explicit choices, is where the modern account closes the loop.

title: Generative Models as Transport: History and Validation
text:
The refined thesis






What we actually teach



Many generative samplers can be represented as maps or stochastic kernels carrying a reference law to the model law — a useful common language, not a complete characterization of generative modeling. On the real line, the total order selects a canonical quantile coupling; for atomless sources it is induced by the unique nondecreasing map, which is simultaneously optimal for every convex displacement cost. Other transports exist even there. In higher dimensions, endpoint marginals underdetermine both the coupling and the dynamics, so additional structure — a cost and its geometry (Brenier), a coordinate order (Knothe–Rosenblatt, autoregressive flows), a forward corruption process together with a choice of probability current (diffusion), an endpoint coupling and interpolant (flow matching, rectified flow, stochastic interpolants), path-space entropy (Schrödinger bridges), or merely an architecture and an objective (GANs, VAEs) — selects the construction. Exact scalar ODE samplers necessarily implement the quantile map, because non-crossing on a line is the order selection; adversarial and variational objectives do not select it, and stochastic decoders and reverse SDEs are kernels, not inverse maps. Dimension one is therefore a laboratory for separating four questions — endpoint matching, transport selection, dynamics, and learnability — not a setting in which the model families are intrinsically identical.
